meta.blurb: A penniless teenager arrives at a school and is told to sweep a room. He cleans it three times. Booker T. Washington, born a slave, tells how that test led to Tuskegee, a school he began with no land and no building.
meta.bible: Booker Washington: born enslaved on a small farm near Hale's Ford, Franklin County, Virginia, about 1856; the founder of Tuskegee; died on 14 November 1915. Jane: his mother, the cook on the farm. John: his older brother. Washington Ferguson: his stepfather, who worked in the salt furnaces of Malden. Viola Ruffner: the strict Vermont-born woman of Malden who taught him thoroughness. Mary Mackie: the Hampton teacher who tested him with a room to sweep. General Samuel Armstrong: the founder of Hampton Institute and Booker's inspiration. Hampton Institute: the school in Virginia where Booker studied and taught. Malden: the West Virginia town of the salt furnaces. Tuskegee: the town in Alabama where Booker opened his school on 4 July 1881. Olivia Davidson: a gifted teacher who helped build Tuskegee. General Marshall: the Hampton treasurer who lent five hundred dollars. Porter Hall: the first big brick building. Aunt Caroline Smith: the old woman who gave six eggs. George Washington Carver: the scientist who joined Tuskegee in 1896. Grover Cleveland: the President who praised the Atlanta speech. William McKinley: the President who visited Tuskegee in 1898. Theodore Roosevelt: the President who invited Booker to dinner in 1901. William Du Bois (written W E B Du Bois in the pages): a scholar who first praised the Atlanta speech and later criticised Booker's views. Atlanta Exposition: the fair of September 1895 where Booker gave his famous speech. National Negro Business League: the group he founded in 1900. Harvard: the university that gave him an honorary degree in 1896. Virginia. West Virginia. Alabama. Richmond. Boston. Atlanta. Vermont. Cotton States. Negro Conference: the farmers' meeting begun in 1892. Up From Slavery: the title of the book, published in 1901. Union. Native American. Webster. Booker Taliaferro Washington: his full name. Fannie Smith: a young woman of Malden, his first wife; they married in 1882 and she died about two years later. Portia: his daughter by Fannie, born in 1883. Amanda: his sister. James: an orphan boy his mother adopted; John and James also went to Hampton. General Lewis Ruffner: owner of the Malden salt furnace and the coal mine; Viola was his wife. Lewis Adams: a tinsmith, once enslaved, and a leader of Tuskegee's Black community who worked for a school. George Campbell: a white businessman of Tuskegee who worked with him. Butler Chapel: the old church in Tuskegee beside the shanty where the school opened. Black Belt: the region of dark soil and large Black population where Tuskegee lies. Wayland Seminary: the school in Washington where Booker studied in 1878. Miss Nathalie Lord: the Hampton teacher who trained his speaking voice. The Wigwam: the Hampton dormitory of the Native American students, where Booker lived as house father. The Plucky Class: the night-school students who worked all day. Mr Porter: a friend of the school in Brooklyn whose gift paid for Porter Hall. Margaret Murray: a Fisk graduate who came to Tuskegee in 1889 as Lady Principal and later became his third wife. Warren Logan: a Hampton graduate who became the school's treasurer. Macon County: the Alabama county where Tuskegee stands. Slater Fund: a fund set up to help the education of freed people. Rufus Bullock: a former governor of Georgia who introduced Booker at the Atlanta Exposition on 18 September 1895. The Oaks: the house the students built for Booker and his family. Voice and tone: honest, humble and warm, with quiet humour; facts stated plainly and without gore; the book is a hopeful life story, and where historians disagree about his ideas or the dates the retelling says so.

beats.scene: A small Virginia farm with a cabin and fields under a summer sky
beats.summary: Booker is born into slavery on a small farm near Hale's Ford, Virginia, around 1856, and never learns his birthday.

beats.scene: A one-room cabin with a dirt floor, a fireplace and no glass windows
beats.summary: His home is a cabin that is also the farm's kitchen, with a dirt floor and no glass in the windows.

beats.scene: A woman cooks over an open fire while children watch from the shadows
beats.summary: His mother, Jane, cooks for everyone on the farm over an open fire, because the cabin has no stove.

beats.scene: Children sleep on a heap of rags beside the dying fire
beats.summary: The children sleep on rags on the floor and eat scraps when they can, with no table and no family meals.

beats.scene: Three children play together in a dusty farmyard
beats.summary: Booker has an older brother, John, and a sister, Amanda, and the three children are always close.

beats.scene: A small boy squirms in a long rough shirt as his brother watches
beats.summary: The flax shirt Booker must wear scratches like pins, until John kindly wears it first to soften it.

beats.scene: Heavy wooden-soled shoes stand by a cabin door in winter
beats.summary: In winter Booker wears hard shoes with wooden soles, which hurt his feet and make a clatter.

beats.scene: A small boy on a horse struggles with a heavy sack of corn
beats.summary: Booker is sent to the mill with a sack of corn, and the sack slips off the horse.

beats.scene: A boy carries books behind a girl on a country road
beats.summary: He carries his young mistress's books to a schoolhouse and sees children studying, which seems like paradise.

beats.scene: A woman kneels over a sleeping boy in a dark cabin
beats.summary: One night his mother kneels beside him and prays that Lincoln's army will win and set her children free.

beats.scene: A bare farm table with little food as the war drags on
beats.summary: As the war drags on, food, cloth and coffee grow scarce even on a small farm like Booker's.

beats.scene: Freed people gather before a farmhouse as a man reads a paper
beats.summary: In 1865 a stranger reads a long paper to the people of the farm, telling them that they are free.

beats.scene: A mother weeps and hugs her three children outside a cabin
beats.summary: Booker's mother kisses her children with tears of joy and says that Lincoln and his army have brought freedom.

beats.scene: An old man hesitates at a farm gate holding a small bundle
beats.summary: After the first joy comes worry, because freed families have no land, no money and no homes, and some old people hesitate to leave.

beats.scene: A family at a table chooses new names by lamplight
beats.summary: Freedom raises small questions as well as big ones, and families begin choosing new names for themselves.

beats.scene: A loaded wagon rolls down a country road at sunrise
beats.summary: The family sets out for Malden, West Virginia, where his stepfather, Washington Ferguson, has found work in the salt works.

beats.scene: A family camps beside a road under the stars with a small fire
beats.summary: The journey takes many days, with the children walking beside the wagon and sleeping in the open at night.

beats.scene: A crowded valley town with salt furnaces and smoke along a river
beats.summary: Malden is a rough, crowded town in a valley full of furnaces, and the family's new cabin is in a poor, noisy corner of it.

beats.scene: A boy shovels salt in the dark beside barrels stamped with a number
beats.summary: Booker and John go to work packing salt in the furnace, starting long before sunrise.

beats.scene: A boy chalks the figure eighteen on the top of a barrel
beats.summary: Booker learns to recognise and write the number eighteen, his stepfather's number, and dreams of reading.

beats.scene: A boy studies a blue spelling book by candlelight while his mother watches
beats.summary: Booker's mother somehow gets him a spelling book, and he teaches himself the alphabet without any teacher.

beats.scene: A young teacher arrives in a crowded cabin where families gather to greet him
beats.summary: A young Black teacher from Ohio comes to Malden, and the whole settlement is wild with joy.

beats.scene: A stepfather shakes his head as a boy pleads at the cabin table
beats.summary: Ferguson says the family needs Booker's wages, and the boy is bitterly disappointed that he cannot go to school.

beats.scene: A tired boy in work clothes slips into a crowded classroom
beats.summary: At last Booker goes to school by working first and arriving afterwards, tired but glad.

beats.scene: A teacher with a roll book looks at a boy standing in a classroom
beats.summary: At roll call the teacher asks for his full name, and Booker, who has only one, calmly says Washington.

beats.scene: A woman smiles beside a boy writing a long name on paper
beats.summary: Later Booker learns that his mother named him Booker Taliaferro, and he writes the missing name in the middle.

beats.scene: A schoolboy stands proudly in a cap made from two pieces of cloth
beats.summary: The other boys have caps from a shop, but his mother sews one for him out of homespun cloth, and he wears it proudly.

beats.scene: A woman and her children welcome an orphan boy beside the cabin fire
beats.summary: Booker's mother takes in an orphan boy named James, and the little family grows.

beats.scene: A boy with a small lamp walks down a narrow dark mine tunnel
beats.summary: Booker works for a time in a coal mine, where the passages are dark, damp and dangerous.

beats.scene: Two miners rest on a ledge talking while a boy listens
beats.summary: Booker overhears two miners speak of Hampton Institute, a school for Black students hundreds of miles away in Virginia.

beats.scene: A tall stern woman in an apron stands in a spotless parlour
beats.summary: The owner of the salt furnace, General Lewis Ruffner, has a wife, Viola, from Vermont, who is famous in Malden for her strict rules.

beats.scene: A nervous boy stands at a big front door holding his cap
beats.summary: Although other boys have quit her service, Booker is afraid but accepts a job as her houseboy.

beats.scene: A boy scrubs a doorstep while a woman inspects the corners
beats.summary: Mrs Ruffner expects everything to be spotless and in its place, and she checks each job carefully.

beats.scene: A boy sweeps a yard into neat lines as a woman watches
beats.summary: Booker must do a task again until it passes her test, and slowly he begins to see why.

beats.scene: A boy sits at a small desk in a winter schoolroom
beats.summary: She allows him to go to school for a few hours a day in winter, and he studies when his work is done.

beats.scene: A woman hands a boy a book at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Mrs Ruffner sees how eager he is to read and encourages him to study whenever his work is done.

beats.scene: A boy polishes a stove until it shines as a clock ticks
beats.summary: Booker learns cleanliness, promptness and honesty, habits he will teach for the rest of his life.

beats.scene: A boy mends a garden gate carefully with a hammer
beats.summary: He learns that a job is not finished until it is done right, even when no one is watching.

beats.scene: A boy and his mother talk quietly by a cabin window at night
beats.summary: Hampton fills his thoughts, and he saves every coin he can while his mother worries about the distance.

beats.scene: Neighbours press coins into a boy's palm as he holds a small bag
beats.summary: In 1872, at about sixteen, Booker sets out for Hampton with a small bag, a few coins and his family's blessing.

beats.scene: A boy hugs his mother at a cabin door before dawn
beats.summary: Booker says goodbye to his family and begins the long journey to Hampton, hundreds of miles away.

beats.scene: A stagecoach climbs a mountain road with a boy on the seat
beats.summary: He travels part of the way by stagecoach through the mountains, and part of it on foot as his money runs low.

beats.scene: A tired boy is turned away at the door of a roadside inn
beats.summary: A roadside inn refuses him a bed because he is Black, and he learns how hard the road will be.

beats.scene: A weary boy walks along a lamplit city street at night
beats.summary: Weak and hungry, he reaches Richmond after dark with no money, no friends and nowhere to sleep.

beats.scene: A boy lies under a wooden sidewalk as footsteps pass overhead
beats.summary: He crawls under a wooden sidewalk and sleeps there, hearing footsteps above him all night.

beats.scene: A boy carries iron bars from a ship while a captain watches
beats.summary: In the morning he asks a ship's captain for work and is allowed to help unload the ship for several days.

beats.scene: A boy walks toward a distant school of red brick under a wide sky
beats.summary: With his small wages he goes on to Hampton and sees its great brick buildings, like the promised land.

beats.scene: A dusty boy waits on the steps while students go in and out
beats.summary: Dirty, ragged and tired, he waits while the head teacher, Miss Mary Mackie, attends to others and hardly looks at him.

beats.scene: A woman hands a broom to a boy in an empty classroom
beats.summary: At last she says that the next room needs sweeping and hands him a broom.

beats.scene: A woman rubs a handkerchief along a clean wooden wall
beats.summary: Booker sweeps three times and dusts four times, and she tests the room with her handkerchief and says he will do.

beats.scene: A boy lights a stove in a dim hallway before dawn
beats.summary: Now accepted, Booker becomes a janitor to pay for his board, rising early to light fires and sweep.

beats.scene: A boy stares at two white sheets on a narrow bed
beats.summary: On his first night in a real bed he is puzzled by the two sheets, never having used even one before.

beats.scene: A tall man in a dark uniform stands before rows of students
beats.summary: He meets General Samuel Armstrong, the founder of Hampton, who was born in Hawaii and led Black soldiers in the war.

beats.scene: A general speaks to students gathered in a bright chapel
beats.summary: Armstrong teaches that the happiest people are those who do the most to help others.

beats.scene: Students in uniform march across a green lawn in neat lines
beats.summary: Hampton runs like a small army camp, with bells, drill, uniforms and inspections, and Booker loves the order.

beats.scene: Students saw wood and shape iron in busy workshops
beats.summary: Every student learns to work with his hands, and Booker sees that honest labour has dignity.

beats.scene: A letter and a banknote lie on a plain wooden desk
beats.summary: A kind stranger in Massachusetts pays Booker's school fees, and he works hard to deserve the gift.

beats.scene: A woman teacher reads aloud while students listen
beats.summary: A teacher, Miss Nathalie Lord, trains him to read aloud and to speak clearly, which he never forgets.

beats.scene: Students debate eagerly at a long table in a crowded room
beats.summary: Booker joins the debating society, where he speaks every week and begins to find his voice.

beats.scene: A young man in work clothes carries a heavy load in summer heat
beats.summary: Each summer he finds whatever work he can to pay his bills, and returns in the autumn ready to study.

beats.scene: A row of graduates in dark suits sits in a bright chapel
beats.summary: In 1875 Booker graduates from Hampton after three years of work and study.

beats.scene: A young man steps off a wagon into a crowd of smiling neighbours
beats.summary: He returns to Malden to a joyful welcome from his mother, his brothers and the whole neighbourhood.

beats.scene: Parents talk earnestly with a young man outside a cabin
beats.summary: The Black families of Malden ask him to teach in their school, and he accepts with delight.

beats.scene: Children of all ages crowd into a small schoolroom
beats.summary: In the day school he teaches reading, writing and sums to children of every age, with very few books.

beats.scene: Weary workers in dusty clothes sit at desks by lamplight
beats.summary: In the night school, men and women who have worked twelve hours at the furnaces and mines come to learn their letters.

beats.scene: A teacher shows a child how to wash hands and comb hair
beats.summary: Booker insists on cleanliness, combed hair and tidy clothes, as Mrs Ruffner and Hampton had taught him.

beats.scene: Neighbours sit around a table of newspapers in a small room
beats.summary: He also opens a reading room and a debating society, and teaches in Sunday schools.

beats.scene: Two young men with bags walk beside Booker toward a station
beats.summary: He helps his brothers John and James, and some of his best pupils, to go to Hampton.

beats.scene: A crowd gathers around a speaker standing on a wagon
beats.summary: These are the years of Reconstruction, when Black men vote and hold office for the first time, and politics is the talk of every town.

beats.scene: A young man in a worn coat studies a Latin book by a window
beats.summary: Booker sees that some people think a degree is a ticket out of hard work, and he begins to wonder what education is truly for.

beats.scene: A young man studies at a desk in a city seminary
beats.summary: In 1878 Booker goes to Washington to study for several months at Wayland Seminary.

beats.scene: Well-dressed young men lean on a railing in a city street
beats.summary: In the capital he sees some young men who spend borrowed money on fine clothes while waiting for government jobs.

beats.scene: A young man looks from a desk toward a church and a courthouse
beats.summary: He wonders for a time whether he should become a minister, but nothing is settled.

beats.scene: A man reads a letter by lamplight in a small room
beats.summary: General Armstrong writes to invite him back to Hampton to give the graduates' speech in June 1879.

beats.scene: A young man speaks to a packed hall of students and guests
beats.summary: The speech goes well, and Booker feels his confidence grow.

beats.scene: A general shakes hands with a young teacher on a green lawn
beats.summary: Armstrong offers him a post at Hampton, teaching Native American students and running a night school.

beats.scene: Young men in blankets and uniforms stand outside a brick dormitory
beats.summary: Dozens of young Native Americans from the West live in a dormitory called the Wigwam, and Booker lives among them as house father.

beats.scene: A teacher shows English words on a blackboard to Native students
beats.summary: The students come from different nations and speak little English, so Booker teaches them, and the changes at Hampton are not easy for them.

beats.scene: Tired young men in work clothes enter a lamplit classroom at night
beats.summary: Booker starts a night school for poor students who work all day in the school's shops and study in the evening, and they are called the Plucky Class.

beats.scene: A tall general and a young teacher walk together beside the water
beats.summary: Armstrong's trust in Booker grows, and Booker is so happy at Hampton that he expects to stay there for ever.

beats.scene: Two men talk beside an anvil in a small Alabama workshop
beats.summary: In Tuskegee, Alabama, Lewis Adams, a skilled tinsmith who was once enslaved, and George Campbell, a white businessman, both want a school for Black children.

beats.scene: A craftsman and a politician shake hands outside a courthouse
beats.summary: As historians tell it, Adams helps to win Black votes for a candidate who promises a school, and the state agrees to pay two thousand dollars a year for teachers.

beats.scene: A letter is sealed and handed to a rider at a post office
beats.summary: The two men write to General Armstrong at Hampton to ask him to recommend a principal, and they expect him to name a white man.

beats.scene: A general sits at a desk reading a letter and thinking
beats.summary: Armstrong replies that he knows of no white man he would recommend, but that he has a young Black teacher in mind.

beats.scene: A telegram is handed to a surprised young man in a school corridor
beats.summary: A telegram arrives from Alabama saying that Booker T Washington will suit them and should be sent at once.

beats.scene: A young man packs a trunk while a general watches
beats.summary: At about twenty-five Booker leaves Hampton, proud, anxious and grateful to the General for his trust.

beats.scene: A train crosses wooded hills toward a small southern station
beats.summary: In June 1881 he travels south into Alabama by train, with every mile bringing him closer to the unknown.

beats.scene: A wide landscape of red fields and small cabins under a bright sky
beats.summary: Tuskegee lies in the Black Belt, a region of rich dark soil where far more Black people than white people live.

beats.scene: A young man stands alone on an empty hillside beside a muddy road
beats.summary: Booker finds no land, no building and no equipment, only the state's promise of money for teachers.

beats.scene: A leaning church and a crooked shanty stand side by side
beats.summary: The only places offered are an old church called Butler Chapel and a poor shanty beside it.

beats.scene: A young principal rides a cart past small cabins and cotton fields
beats.summary: Before opening his school, Booker spends a month travelling the countryside by cart to see how people really live.

beats.scene: A crowded one-room cabin with a family around a small table
beats.summary: He visits one-room cabins where whole families sleep in a single room and eat pork and cornbread.

beats.scene: A shiny organ stands in the corner of a bare, dark cabin
beats.summary: In one cabin he sees an expensive organ that nobody can play, bought on credit by a family that has little else.

beats.scene: Farmers hand cotton to a storekeeper who writes in a thick ledger
beats.summary: He learns how many farmers rent their land and buy supplies on credit, and end every year owing the whole crop.

beats.scene: A log schoolhouse with a few pupils and a tired teacher
beats.summary: The country schools run for only a few months a year, in poor buildings with few books.

beats.scene: A young principal and an old farmer lean on a fence and talk
beats.summary: Booker decides that the school must teach people how to live, farm and build, as well as how to read.

beats.scene: A hand-lettered notice is pinned to a church door
beats.summary: On 4 July 1881 the school opens in the old church and the shanty beside it.

beats.scene: Thirty students sit in a plain room while rain drips from the ceiling
beats.summary: About thirty students arrive, and many are grown men and women who are already teachers.

beats.scene: Students line up with toothbrushes and clean hands before a teacher
beats.summary: Booker insists that every student must have a toothbrush, a bath and a tidy bed, as part of the school's lessons.

beats.scene: A woman in a plain dress arrives with a trunk at the church door
beats.summary: Olivia Davidson, a gifted teacher, arrives to join him, and the school now has two teachers.

beats.scene: An abandoned plantation of weeds and gullies with an old burnt house
beats.summary: The school soon needs more room, and an abandoned plantation of about a hundred acres, a short way from town, is for sale.

beats.scene: A young principal writes a letter at a candlelit table
beats.summary: Booker writes to General Marshall, the treasurer at Hampton, who sends five hundred dollars for the first payment.

beats.scene: Worn fields cut by gullies and thick brush under a grey sky
beats.summary: The land is worn out by years of cotton, the big house burned down long ago, and only a few poor outbuildings remain.

beats.scene: A group of students stands with folded arms beside a bush-covered hill
beats.summary: Some students say they came to study books, not to work in fields, and the principal must change their minds.

beats.scene: A young principal swings an axe among the bushes as students watch
beats.summary: Booker takes an axe himself and begins to clear the land, and the students soon follow.

beats.scene: Students cut brush and pile it into heaps on a hillside
beats.summary: For weeks the students cut bushes, burn heaps and grub out roots until the old fields are ready to plough.

beats.scene: Students plant seeds in freshly ploughed rows on a bright morning
beats.summary: They plant crops that will help to feed the school, and learn farming by doing it.

beats.scene: An old stable and kitchen are cleaned and filled with benches and desks
beats.summary: The old kitchen, the stable and the hen-house are cleaned out and used as classrooms and workrooms.

beats.scene: People in their best clothes eat at long tables at a school supper
beats.summary: Olivia Davidson organises suppers and festivals to raise money, and Black and white neighbours come to them.

beats.scene: A young principal sits awake at night counting coins by a candle
beats.summary: Booker lies awake worrying about debts and payments, but the kindness of neighbours gives him courage.

beats.scene: Students crowd into a hen-house classroom while rain falls outside
beats.summary: The school keeps growing and needs a proper building, so Booker decides that the students will make the bricks themselves.

beats.scene: A pit of wet red clay with students pressing bricks into wooden moulds
beats.summary: They dig clay, press it into wooden moulds and set the soft bricks out to dry, though nobody knows how to burn them.

beats.scene: A stack of raw bricks in a smoking, collapsed kiln
beats.summary: The first kiln fails, and the bricks are spoiled.

beats.scene: Students stare at a cracked kiln wall, tired and discouraged
beats.summary: A second kiln fails as well, and some people say that the school should give up the idea.

beats.scene: A young man hands his watch to a pawnbroker across a counter
beats.summary: Booker pawns his watch for fifteen dollars to pay for a third attempt.

beats.scene: A kiln glows at night as tired students tend the fire
beats.summary: For days and nights the students tend the fires, and nobody dares to sleep.

beats.scene: Students carefully open a cooled kiln and find red bricks inside
beats.summary: When the kiln cools, the bricks are good, and the school cheers.

beats.scene: A wagon is loaded with red bricks for sale in town
beats.summary: Tuskegee bricks are sold to townspeople, and brickmaking becomes both a trade and an income.

beats.scene: A student stands proudly beside a wall made of his own bricks
beats.summary: Students who learn brickmaking gain a skill they can use anywhere, and Booker sees that learning by doing works.

beats.scene: Students dig a long trench for the foundation of a large building
beats.summary: Booker plans the school's first large building, to be made with bricks the students have baked.

beats.scene: A letter with a bank note arrives on a school desk
beats.summary: A generous friend of the school in Brooklyn, Mr Porter, gives money for the first large building, which will carry his name.

beats.scene: Students lay red bricks in a long line on a foundation wall
beats.summary: The students lay the walls with the bricks they made, learning the work of a mason as they go.

beats.scene: Students saw timber and fit window frames in a busy workshop
beats.summary: Others cut the wood and build doors and window frames, learning carpentry by making real parts of a real house.

beats.scene: A principal frowns over a pile of bills beside a few coins
beats.summary: Lumber, nails and glass cost money, and Booker is always close to running out, so he pays each bill as soon as he can.

beats.scene: Scaffolding rises around brick walls as students carry loads up ladders
beats.summary: The walls rise higher week by week, and the whole school watches the building grow.

beats.scene: A finished brick building with a flag stands against a blue sky
beats.summary: Porter Hall is finished, with classrooms and rooms for living, and the students are proud of what they have built.

beats.scene: Students stuff straw into cloth sacks to make mattresses
beats.summary: The students make their own beds and mattresses, since they must make them before they can sleep on them.

beats.scene: Students set a long table with plates, forks and a white cloth
beats.summary: Booker insists on tables, cloths, plates and good manners, and meals become lessons in everyday life.

beats.scene: A young man and woman stand before a minister in a small church
beats.summary: In 1882 Booker marries Fannie Smith of Malden, whom he has known since boyhood.

beats.scene: A young mother holds a baby girl in a sunlit cabin doorway
beats.summary: Their daughter Portia is born in 1883, but Fannie dies about two years after the wedding, and Booker returns to his work with a heavy heart.

beats.scene: A frail woman in a plain dress speaks in a Northern parlour
beats.summary: Olivia Davidson travels north to raise money and returns with gifts, though her health is weak.

beats.scene: A young man and woman stand together with two small boys
beats.summary: Booker and Olivia marry and have two sons, and she goes on working for the school while raising them.

beats.scene: A school flag hangs at half-mast above a silent campus
beats.summary: In 1889 Olivia dies after years of overwork, and Tuskegee mourns the woman who had done so much for it.

beats.scene: A young woman teacher in a plain dress opens a classroom door
beats.summary: Margaret Murray, a graduate of Fisk University, comes to Tuskegee in 1889 as Lady Principal.

beats.scene: A thin man writes figures in a ledger beside a window
beats.summary: Warren Logan, a Hampton graduate, joins the school and becomes its treasurer, and teachers work for very small pay.

beats.scene: Students in a bright chapel sing together at evening prayers
beats.summary: At evening prayers the students sing the old spirituals, and the singing becomes a loved tradition.

beats.scene: A well-dressed Black traveller is turned away at a hotel desk
beats.summary: On his journeys Booker is sometimes refused a hotel room or a seat on a train, and he decides never to hate.

beats.scene: A principal walks across the campus and looks at the grounds
beats.summary: He walks the grounds and visits rooms himself, because he believes that small things show a school's character.

beats.scene: Students in work clothes carry tools toward the fields and shops
beats.summary: Every student works with his hands each day, and the labour pays part of the cost of his education.

beats.scene: Tired students in work clothes enter a lamplit classroom at night
beats.summary: As at Hampton, students who cannot pay may work by day and study in a night school.

beats.scene: A train rolls north through autumn fields at dusk
beats.summary: The school needs money for land, buildings and salaries, so Booker spends long months travelling north by train to ask for help.

beats.scene: A young man speaks quietly to a small audience in a church
beats.summary: He speaks in churches and parlours, telling the plain story of the school without begging.

beats.scene: A principal shows a ledger and photographs to two visitors
beats.summary: He keeps honest accounts, shows what has been done with every gift and invites donors to come and see.

beats.scene: A rich man listens politely at a desk and shakes his head
beats.summary: Many doors stay closed and many people give nothing, but Booker returns politely and does not lose heart.

beats.scene: An old woman hands six eggs to a young principal at her cabin door
beats.summary: An elderly woman, Aunt Caroline Smith, who is very poor, gives the school six eggs, and the gift touches him deeply.

beats.scene: A teacher writes thank-you letters at a lamplit desk
beats.summary: Booker writes a letter of thanks to every giver, large or small.

beats.scene: Northern visitors walk beside students at work in the fields
beats.summary: Visitors from the North come to Tuskegee and see the students at work for themselves.

beats.scene: A man in a dark coat reads a letter bearing a seal
beats.summary: In later years a fund set up to help the education of freed people, the Slater Fund, gives grants that help pay teachers.

beats.scene: A tired man sleeps sitting upright in a railway carriage seat
beats.summary: The travelling is exhausting, with night trains and cold waiting rooms, but every journey adds to the school.

beats.scene: A new brick dormitory rises beside Porter Hall as students work
beats.summary: With gifts from the North, new buildings begin to rise beside Porter Hall.

beats.scene: Students work at anvils, benches and printing presses in busy workshops
beats.summary: Tuskegee adds more trades, including carpentry, blacksmithing, printing, shoemaking, harness making and tailoring.

beats.scene: A young architect unrolls a plan for a new brick building
beats.summary: Robert Taylor, a trained Black architect, joins the school in 1892 and plans many of its buildings.

beats.scene: A principal writes invitations to farmers at a crowded desk
beats.summary: Booker invites the farmers and workers of the area to a meeting, so that neighbours can talk about their common problems.

beats.scene: Wagons and mules crowd a school yard as farmers arrive in their best clothes
beats.summary: In February 1892 about four hundred men and women come to the first Tuskegee Negro Conference.

beats.scene: A speaker asks questions as farmers raise their hands in a bright hall
beats.summary: Booker asks plain questions about land, debt, houses and schools, and the farmers answer honestly.

beats.scene: An old farmer stands to tell his story while others nod
beats.summary: Farmers speak frankly about their debts, their rents and the crops that earn the most.

beats.scene: Farmers ride home in wagons with notes and new plans
beats.summary: They go home with practical ideas, and the conference becomes a yearly event that spreads to other places.

beats.scene: A portrait of a general draped in black hangs in a chapel
beats.summary: In 1893 General Armstrong, who has been ill for some time, dies, and Booker mourns his teacher and model.

beats.scene: Students carry a plain coffin through a school graveyard under tall trees
beats.summary: Armstrong is buried at Hampton among the students he loved, and Booker remembers all that he learned from him.

beats.scene: A wedding in a school chapel with students looking on
beats.summary: In 1893 Booker marries Margaret Murray, who becomes his steady partner and leads the school's work for women.

beats.scene: The Atlanta fair grounds with new halls, flags and crowds
beats.summary: In 1895 Atlanta plans a great fair, the Cotton States and International Exposition, to show the progress of the South, with a building for the work of Black Americans.

beats.scene: A young principal speaks before a committee of congressmen in a marble hall
beats.summary: Earlier, Booker speaks in Washington before a committee of Congress in support of the fair, and impresses the Atlanta organisers.

beats.scene: Two men from Atlanta hand an invitation to a surprised principal
beats.summary: The directors of the Exposition invite him to speak on the opening day, and he accepts.

beats.scene: A man sits alone at a desk with a pile of letters
beats.summary: Booker knows that he has two audiences, and that each one has fears about what he will say.

beats.scene: A man writes and rewrites a page at a lamplit desk
beats.summary: He writes the speech with great care, discarding and rewriting until he is satisfied.

beats.scene: Students and teachers gather at a campus gate to wave off a train
beats.summary: Tuskegee wishes him well, and he leaves for Atlanta and sleeps very little.

beats.scene: A crowded Atlanta street with banners and a parade on a hot morning
beats.summary: On the opening day of the Exposition the streets are full of banners, bands and crowds.

beats.scene: A man in a dark suit sits among officials on a high platform
beats.summary: On the platform he sits among governors and Southern leaders, one of the first Black men to speak at such an event.

beats.scene: An elderly white official introduces a Black speaker to a vast hall
beats.summary: Governor Rufus Bullock introduces him to the crowd, and the hall applauds.

beats.scene: A hush falls over a huge crowd as a man begins to speak
beats.summary: Booker begins by reminding everyone that a third of the South is Black.

beats.scene: A speaker with an open hand addresses a packed hall
beats.summary: Booker tells the crowd that no part of the South can succeed without the other, and that Black and white people share one future.

beats.scene: A ship at sea signals to another ship with flags
beats.summary: He tells a story of a ship lost at sea whose crew signal that they are dying of thirst, and are told again and again to cast down their bucket where they are.

beats.scene: Sailors lower a bucket and pull up fresh water at a river mouth
beats.summary: At last the captain obeys, and the bucket comes up full of fresh water from the mouth of the Amazon River.

beats.scene: A farmer, a carpenter and a cook work side by side
beats.summary: To Black listeners he says: start where you are, in farming, trades, housework and business, and do your work well.

beats.scene: White businessmen listen as a speaker points toward the nearby streets
beats.summary: To white listeners he says: look to the neighbours who have worked your fields and built your railroads, and give them a fair chance.

beats.scene: A hand with five fingers is held open and then closed into a fist
beats.summary: He says that in social matters the races can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in everything that helps all to progress.

beats.scene: A farmer and a poet face each other across a field, both smiling
beats.summary: He says that no race can prosper until it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem.

beats.scene: A cheering crowd waves hats and handkerchiefs in a vast hall
beats.summary: The crowd cheers, waving hats and handkerchiefs, and Governor Bullock hurries across the platform to shake his hand.

beats.scene: Newspaper presses print headlines about a speaker's address
beats.summary: Newspapers across the country print the speech, and President Grover Cleveland writes a letter of congratulation.

beats.scene: Two men argue politely in a library, one holding the printed speech
beats.summary: Some Black leaders say that the speech gave up too much on voting rights and equal treatment, and the argument goes on.

beats.scene: A man in an academic gown receives a certificate in a tree-lined yard
beats.summary: In 1896 Harvard gives Booker an honorary degree, a rare honour for a Black American at that time.

beats.scene: A young scientist arrives at a railway station carrying a small case
beats.summary: That year George Washington Carver, a trained scientist who was born into slavery, comes to Tuskegee to teach agriculture.

beats.scene: A scientist examines plants and soil jars in a small laboratory
beats.summary: Carver makes a laboratory from simple things, teaches farmers to rest their soil with crops such as peanuts, and writes bulletins for them.

beats.scene: A speaker talks calmly to one listener in a crowded hall
beats.summary: Booker explains his idea of public speaking: have something to say, forget yourself and speak plainly to the listeners.

beats.scene: A packed hall in Chicago listens to a speaker while a President sits nearby
beats.summary: In October 1898 he speaks at a peace celebration in Chicago and praises the Black soldiers of the war with Spain.

beats.scene: A president steps from a carriage onto a school campus
beats.summary: In December 1898 President William McKinley visits Tuskegee with members of his cabinet.

beats.scene: A president walks past lines of students at work in shops and fields
beats.summary: The visitors watch the students at work in the classrooms, shops and fields, and McKinley praises the school.

beats.scene: A steamship leaves a harbour with a man and woman at the rail
beats.summary: In 1899 friends urge Booker to rest after years of overwork, and he sails for Europe with his wife.

beats.scene: Strangers greet a Black traveller politely on a European street
beats.summary: In Europe Booker is treated with courtesy in hotels and on the street, and he finds it a welcome change.

beats.scene: A man steps off a train to a crowd of cheering students
beats.summary: He comes home rested and thankful, and he returns to his work at Tuskegee with new ideas.

beats.scene: Men in dark suits gather around a long table in a Boston hall
beats.summary: In 1900 Booker founds the National Negro Business League in Boston to encourage Black-owned businesses.

beats.scene: A shop owner, a farmer and a banker shake hands at a meeting
beats.summary: The League grows, with branches in many towns, and business owners share ideas and give each other courage.

beats.scene: A man writes at a desk in the early morning beside stacked pages
beats.summary: Booker writes his life story, which first appears in a magazine in 1900, with help from friends and editors.

beats.scene: A plain-covered book lies on a table beside a lamp
beats.summary: Up From Slavery is published as a book in 1901, becomes very popular and is later translated into many languages.

beats.scene: A president sits at a long dinner table with an African American guest
beats.summary: In October 1901 President Theodore Roosevelt invites Booker to dinner at the White House, and many white Southerners are furious.

beats.scene: A president and a Black educator talk quietly in a study
beats.summary: Roosevelt sometimes asks Booker's advice, and Booker's influence grows, along with the number of his critics.

beats.scene: A young scholar and an older man argue over a book
beats.summary: In 1903 W E B Du Bois publishes a book that criticises Booker's approach, and later groups demand a faster fight for equal rights.

beats.scene: A tired man travels south on a train with a doctor beside him
beats.summary: In 1915, ill and exhausted, Booker collapses in New York and asks to be taken home to Tuskegee, where he dies on 14 November.

beats.scene: A long line of mourners follows a coffin across a campus of red brick
beats.summary: Thousands of people honour him at his funeral, and he is buried on the campus near the buildings his students built.

beats.scene: Students walk across a modern campus past old brick buildings in the afternoon sun
beats.summary: Today Tuskegee is a university and a national historic site, and his book is still read and argued over.

A1A2: Booker was born a slave on a small farm in Virginia.
His home was a little cabin with a dirt floor.
His mother, Jane, cooked all the meals for the farm.
The children slept on old rags on the cold floor.
Booker had an older brother, John, and a sister, Amanda.
Booker's new shirt was rough, and it hurt his skin.
In winter Booker wore heavy shoes made with wooden soles.
Little Booker carried corn to the mill on a horse.
Booker walked behind the girl and carried her school books.
At night his mother prayed for Mr Lincoln and his army.
During the war, the farm had less food and less cloth.
One day a man read a paper to the slaves.
Booker's mother cried, kissed her children and said they were free.
The new freedom was good, but nobody had land or money.
After freedom, families began to choose new names for themselves.
Booker's family went to West Virginia to join his stepfather.
The family walked beside the wagon and slept outside at night.
Malden was a crowded town with many busy salt furnaces.
Booker and John worked in the salt furnace before the sun came up.
Booker learned to write the number eighteen on the barrels.
His mother found a spelling book, and Booker learned his letters.
A young teacher came to Malden, and everybody was happy.
Booker's stepfather said the family needed his money, not his school.
Booker worked first and then went to school after work.
The teacher asked his name, and Booker said, “Washington.”
His mother told him he was really Booker Taliaferro Washington.
Booker had no cap, so his mother made one for him.
His mother took in a little orphan boy named James.
Booker worked in a dark, wet, dangerous coal mine.
In the mine, Booker heard about a school called Hampton.
Mrs Ruffner, the owner's wife, was very strict about everything.
Many boys had quit her house, but Booker took the job.
She wanted every room clean and every thing in its place.
Booker did each job again until she was happy.
In winter, Mrs Ruffner let him go to school for some hours.
She told him to keep reading and to keep learning.
Booker learned to be clean, on time and honest.
He learned that a job is not finished until it is right.
Booker kept thinking about Hampton and saved every coin he could.
At sixteen, Booker left home with a small bag and a few coins.
Booker said goodbye to his mother and began the long journey.
He rode in a coach, and later he walked.
An inn would not give a bed to Booker.
He reached Richmond at night with no money and no friends.
Booker slept under a wooden sidewalk and heard feet above him.
In the morning, a ship's captain gave him work.
At last Booker saw the big brick school at Hampton.
Booker was dirty, tired and hungry, and the teacher waited.
Then the teacher gave him a broom and said, “Sweep that room.”
She checked the room and said, “I think you will do.”
Booker became a janitor and got up early to light the fires.
On his first night, Booker did not know how to use two sheets.
Booker met General Armstrong, the founder of the school.
The General said that happy people help other people.
At Hampton, everything ran on time, and Booker loved the order.
Every student learned to work with his hands at Hampton.
A kind man in Massachusetts paid for Booker's school fees.
A teacher showed Booker how to read aloud and speak clearly.
Booker joined a group where students argued about big questions.
In summer, Booker did any job he could to pay his bills.
In 1875, Booker finished his studies at Hampton and graduated.
Booker went home to Malden, and everyone was glad to see him.
The people of Malden asked Booker to teach their school.
In the day, Booker taught children to read, write and count.
At night, tired workers came to Booker's school to learn.
Booker taught the children to wash and to comb their hair.
Booker started a reading room and a club for debates.
Booker helped his brothers and some pupils go to Hampton.
In those years, Black men could vote, and everyone talked about politics.
Booker wondered what education was really for.
In 1878, Booker went to Washington to study for some months.
In the capital, Booker saw young men who spent money on fine clothes.
Booker thought for a while about becoming a minister.
General Armstrong wrote and asked Booker to speak at Hampton.
Booker gave his speech, and it went very well.
The General asked Booker to come back and teach at Hampton.
Booker lived with young Native American students in a house called the Wigwam.
Booker taught English to the Native American students.
Booker started a night school for students who worked all day.
Booker was happy at Hampton and trusted by the General.
Two men in Tuskegee, Mr Adams and Mr Campbell, wanted a school.
The state promised money to pay teachers for the new school.
They wrote to General Armstrong and asked him for a principal.
The General said he knew a good young Black teacher.
A telegram came from Alabama and said, “Send Booker at once.”
Booker packed his trunk and left Hampton at twenty-five.
In June 1881, Booker took a train south to Alabama.
Tuskegee was in the Black Belt, where most people were Black.
In Tuskegee, Booker found no land, no building and no books.
There was only an old church and a tiny, poor house.
Booker spent a month visiting the poor families of the area.
Many families lived and slept in only one small room.
One family owned an expensive organ, but nobody could play it.
Farmers owed money to the store at the end of every year.
The country schools were open for only a few months.
Booker decided the school must teach people how to live.
On 4 July 1881, the school opened in the old church.
About thirty students came, and some were already teachers.
Booker told every student to use a toothbrush and keep clean.
Olivia Davidson came to Tuskegee to teach with Booker.
An old, worn-out farm near town was for sale.
Booker wrote to Hampton, and a friend sent five hundred dollars.
The land was poor, and the old house had burned down.
Some students said they came to study, not to dig.
Booker picked up an axe, and the students followed him.
For weeks, the students cut bushes and cleared the fields.
The students planted crops to feed the school.
They cleaned the old kitchen and stable and used them as classrooms.
Miss Davidson held suppers to raise money for the school.
Booker lay awake at night and worried about the school's debts.
The school needed a real building, so Booker planned to make bricks.
The students dug clay and pressed it into wooden moulds.
The first fire failed, and the bricks were ruined.
The second fire failed too, and many people lost hope.
Booker sold his watch to pay for a third try.
For days and nights, the students watched the fire.
At last the bricks were good, and everyone cheered.
The school sold bricks to people in the town.
The students learned a real trade by making bricks.
Next, the students began to dig for a big new building.
A friend in Brooklyn, Mr Porter, sent money for a big building.
The students laid the red bricks that they had made.
Other students cut wood and made doors and windows.
Booker had many bills, and he paid each one quickly.
The walls grew higher each week, and everyone watched.
Porter Hall was finished, and the students felt proud.
The students made their own beds from cloth and straw.
Booker wanted tables, plates and good manners at every meal.
In 1882, Booker married Fannie Smith from Malden.
Their daughter Portia was born, but Fannie died soon afterwards.
Miss Davidson went north to ask for money for the school.
Booker married Olivia Davidson, and they had two sons.
In 1889, Olivia died, and the whole school was sad.
Margaret Murray came to Tuskegee in 1889 to teach.
Warren Logan became the school's treasurer and kept its money.
In the evenings, the students sang old songs in the chapel.
Booker was sometimes refused a hotel room, but he never hated anyone.
Booker walked around the school and looked at every small thing.
Every student did some work with his hands each day.
At night, poor students came to class after a day of work.
The school needed money, so Booker travelled north by train.
In churches, Booker told people the true story of the school.
Booker kept honest accounts and showed donors how he spent money.
Many people said no, but Booker did not give up.
One poor old woman gave the school six eggs.
Booker wrote a letter of thanks to every giver.
Visitors from the North came to see the school at work.
A fund to help freed people gave money to Tuskegee.
The long journeys were tiring, but each one helped the school.
With gifts from the North, new buildings began to rise.
Tuskegee added more trades, such as building and printing.
In 1892, Robert Taylor came to design buildings for the school.
Booker invited farmers to come to a meeting at Tuskegee.
In 1892, about four hundred people came to the first meeting.
Booker asked plain questions about land, debts and houses.
The farmers told their stories honestly, and many nodded.
The farmers went home with good ideas, and the meeting grew.
In 1893, General Armstrong died, and Booker was very sad.
Armstrong was buried at Hampton among his own students.
In 1893, Booker married Margaret Murray, and she helped him.
In 1895, Atlanta planned a great fair to show the new South.
Booker spoke in Washington to support the fair.
The leaders of the fair asked Booker to speak on opening day.
Booker had two audiences, and each one was afraid.
He wrote the speech with great care and wrote it again.
The school said goodbye, and Booker took the train to Atlanta.
On opening day, the streets of Atlanta were full of people.
Booker sat on the platform with the leaders of the South.
Governor Bullock introduced him, and the crowd clapped.
Booker began, “One third of the South is Black.”
Booker said that the South could not succeed without Black people.
He told a story about a ship in need of water.
The captain cast down his bucket and found fresh water.
Booker told Black people to start work right where they were.
Booker told white people to help their Black neighbours.
He said the two races were like fingers on one hand.
He said that farming is as worthy as writing a poem.
The crowd cheered, and the Governor ran to shake his hand.
Newspapers printed the speech, and the President wrote a kind letter.
Some Black leaders said that the speech gave up too much.
In 1896, Harvard gave Booker a special honour.
George Washington Carver came to Tuskegee in 1896 to teach farming.
Carver showed farmers how to make poor soil good again.
Booker said a speaker should know his subject and be simple.
In 1898, Booker spoke in Chicago in front of the President.
The President of the country came to visit Tuskegee.
The President watched the students work and praised the school.
In 1899, Booker was tired, and friends sent him to Europe.
In Europe, people treated Booker with respect.
Booker came home rested and went back to work.
In 1900, Booker started a group to help Black businesses.
The group grew, and business owners shared good ideas.
Booker wrote the story of his life for a magazine.
In 1901, Up From Slavery came out as a book.
In 1901, President Roosevelt asked Booker to dinner.
The President sometimes asked Booker for his advice.
Some critics said that Booker's plan was too slow.
In 1915, Booker was ill and asked to go home.
He died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915.
Today Tuskegee is a university, and people still read his book.
B1B2: Booker Washington was born a slave on a small farm in Virginia, most likely in 1856. He never knew his exact birthday, and he knew nothing about his white father.
Booker lived with his mother, Jane, in a cabin that was also the farm's kitchen. It had a dirt floor, no glass in the windows, and a hole in the ground where sweet potatoes were kept.
Jane cooked for the whole farm over an open fire, because the cabin had no stove. She worked at all hours, and her children often woke to the smell of smoke and cooking.
There were no beds in the cabin, so the children slept on a pile of rags on the floor. They never sat down to a family dinner, and ate whatever scraps they could find during the day.
Booker had an older brother named John and a sister called Amanda, and the three were never apart. Their cabin was crowded, but it was the one place where they felt safe.
The only shirt Booker owned was made of rough flax, and it felt like a hundred pins on his skin. His brother John, who was a little older, wore it first until the cloth became softer.
In winter the children wore shoes with wooden soles, which were stiff, heavy and very noisy. They were hard to walk in, but without them his feet would have suffered even more in the cold.
When he was still small, Booker was sent to the mill with a sack of corn tied on a horse. The sack slid off, and he was too weak to lift it back, so he waited for a stranger to come along.
Sometimes Booker carried the books of his young mistress to the little schoolhouse. Seeing the children study inside, he thought that going to school must be like paradise.
One night Booker woke up and found his mother kneeling beside him, praying in a low voice. She asked God to let President Lincoln's army win, because that would set her children free.

As the war went on, even the small farm grew poorer, and coffee, sugar and cloth became hard to find. The enslaved people listened for every scrap of news, and they could tell that something was changing.

One morning in 1865, the people of the farm gathered in front of the big house, and a stranger stood up to read a long paper. Booker was a small boy, and he did not understand all the words, but he understood the word free.
His mother bent down and kissed her children, and tears ran down her face. She told them that Mr Lincoln and his soldiers had brought this day, which she had prayed for so many nights.

The joy lasted only a short time, because the freed families soon asked, where do we go now? They had no land, no money and no homes of their own, and many old people were afraid to leave the only place they knew.
Most of the enslaved had only one name, and now they had to decide what to call themselves. Families talked about it for days, and some chose to take new names to show that their old life was over.

Booker's stepfather, Washington Ferguson, had already found work in Malden, West Virginia, and he sent for his family. They packed their few pots and blankets into a wagon, said goodbye to the farm and set off at sunrise.
The journey was long, and the children walked beside the wagon for most of the way. At night they made a fire beside the road, ate what they had brought and slept under the open sky.

Malden lay in a narrow valley full of salt furnaces, where smoke rose all day and barrels moved along the river. The family's cabin stood in a crowded, noisy part of town, and Booker thought it a worse place than the farm.
Booker's stepfather soon found jobs for both boys in the salt furnace. They were nine or ten years old, and they had to start work at four in the morning, long before the sun was up.

Each barrel of salt was marked with the number of the man who had packed it, and Booker's stepfather was number eighteen. Booker copied it again and again until he could write the figure by himself, and it was his first lesson in reading.
Booker's mother could not read, but she found a spelling book for him somewhere. He took it to the cabin every night, and with no teacher to help, he taught himself the whole alphabet.
Then one day a young Black teacher arrived from Ohio, and the whole settlement was excited. The people took turns to give him a room and meals, and each family tried to give him its best food.
Booker begged to go to school, but his stepfather said the family needed his wages from the furnace. It was a bitter disappointment, and for a while the boy thought his dream was finished.
After a time Booker was allowed to study at night, and later he went to the day school as well, on one condition. He had to work at the furnace early in the morning and again when school was over.
On the first day, the teacher called the roll and asked for his full name. Booker had always been called just Booker, but he calmly answered Washington, as if he had used it all his life.
Later he learned that his mother had given him the name Booker Taliaferro when he was born. He was glad to have it, and from then on he wrote the name Taliaferro between the other two.
Most of the boys at school wore caps from a shop, but Booker had nothing to put on his head. His mother sewed two pieces of homespun cloth together, and he wore the cap with pride and without shame.
His mother had a kind heart, and she took in a poor orphan boy called James and brought him up with her own children. The cabin was small and crowded, but there was always room for one more.
Booker did not stay in the furnace for ever, and he spent some time working in a coal mine. The narrow passages were dark and damp, and he was often afraid of the dangers.

One day, deep in the mine, Booker heard two miners talking about a school called Hampton Institute. They said that poor students could work there to pay for their food and lessons, and he never forgot it.
The owner of the salt furnace and the coal mine was General Lewis Ruffner, and his wife was named Viola. She came from Vermont, and everyone in Malden knew that she was the strictest woman in town.
Boy after boy had worked in her house and quit after a few weeks, because nothing was ever good enough for her. Booker was afraid, but he wanted to earn money and learn, so he took the job.
Mrs Ruffner wanted every floor clean, every dish in its place and every task finished on time. She walked around the house looking into corners, and she always noticed what had been missed.

If Booker swept the yard, she looked at it carefully and sent him back if one small thing had been left. At first he thought she was unkind, but little by little he understood that she wanted him to be thorough.
In the winter months, Mrs Ruffner gave him permission to go to school for a few hours a day. He did all his work first and ran to school afterwards, and he was happy to be there.
Mrs Ruffner saw that Booker loved to read, so she encouraged him to study whenever his work was done. It was the first time that anyone with power over him had cheered him on.

Booker worked in her house for about a year and a half, and he learned three things from her that never left him. They were to be clean, to be on time and to be honest, and he later taught them to hundreds of students.
One of her rules was that a job was not finished until it had been done properly. Booker never forgot this, and he tried to work as carefully when nobody was watching as when someone was.
All this time, the thought of Hampton stayed in Booker's mind, and he saved every coin that he could. His mother worried because the school was so far away, but she saw how much it meant to him.

In 1872, when he was about sixteen, Booker packed a small bag with a few clothes and set out for Hampton. Many poor neighbours pressed small coins into his hand, and his family gave him their blessing.
Booker said goodbye to his mother, his brother and his sister, and set off on the long road to Hampton. He had a small bag, very little money and a great hope.
For part of the journey he rode in a stagecoach through the mountains, but the fare was expensive. When his money began to run out, he had to walk, and he asked for rides on wagons whenever he could.
One night, tired and cold, he asked for a bed at a roadside inn, but the owner refused because he was Black. It was a hard lesson, and he spent the night outside with only his courage for company.
At last Booker came to Richmond, the big city of Virginia, late at night. He was hungry and weak, he had no money, and he did not know a single person who could help him.

Walking the dark streets, Booker found a place where the wooden sidewalk was raised above the ground. He crawled underneath and lay there, listening to footsteps going over his head, until he fell asleep.
In the morning he was very hungry, and he saw a ship near the water being unloaded. He asked the captain for work, and the kind man let him carry iron for several days, so that he could buy food.
With the little money he had earned, Booker went on towards Hampton. When he saw the big brick buildings of the school, he felt that he had reached a promised land at last.

Booker was dirty, ragged and tired after the long journey, and he knew that he did not look like a good student. The head teacher, Miss Mary Mackie, said very little to him and was busy with other people, so he waited and wondered.
After a long time, Miss Mackie said that the room next door needed to be swept, and she gave him a broom. Booker was glad, because he knew exactly what to do.

Booker swept the room three times and dusted every piece of furniture four times. Miss Mackie rubbed her handkerchief along the walls and the woodwork, found no dust at all and said quietly that he would do.
Booker was now a student, but he had no money, so he was made the school janitor. He got up before dawn to light the fires and sweep the floors, and he was never late.
That night Booker was shown to a real bed, and it had two white sheets. He had never used even one sheet before, so he slept under both, and the next night he slept on top of both.
The head of the school was General Samuel Armstrong, who had been born in Hawaii and had led Black soldiers in the Civil War. Booker thought he was the noblest man he had ever seen.
The General taught his students that the happiest people are the ones who do the most to help others. Booker listened closely, and he thought about those words for the rest of his life.
Hampton was run almost like an army camp, with bells, drills, uniforms and daily inspections. Booker had never known such order, and he liked it very much.
At Hampton every student had to learn a trade as well as study books. Booker watched the students with pride in their work, and he began to believe that honest labour deserves respect.
Booker could not pay the school fees, but a kind man in Massachusetts agreed to pay them for him. Booker never met him at first, yet he worked hard every day so that the gift would not be wasted.
One of his teachers, Miss Nathalie Lord, taught him how to read aloud and speak clearly. She showed him that a voice can be trained, and he never forgot her lessons.
Booker joined the debating society, where students met every week to argue about important questions. He was nervous at first, but with practice he began to speak with more confidence.
When school ended each summer, Booker had to earn money for the next year. He took whatever work he could find, and each autumn he returned to Hampton, ready to learn again.
In 1875, after three years of study and hard work, Booker graduated from Hampton. A boy who had once packed salt now held a diploma, and he could hardly believe it.
Booker went back to Malden, where his mother, his brothers and the neighbours came out to welcome him. Everyone wanted to see the young man who had gone so far away to school.
The Black families of Malden wanted their children to learn, and they asked Booker to take over their school. He accepted at once, because he wished to give to others what Hampton had given to him.
In the day school, the children came in all sizes, and some were nearly grown. There were very few books, so Booker taught reading, writing and sums in any way he could.

At night the school opened again for men and women who had worked twelve hours at the furnaces and mines. Some were old enough to be Booker's grandparents, yet they sat down and learned their letters with bright eyes.
Booker taught habits as well as lessons from books. He showed the children how to wash, comb their hair and keep their clothes neat, as Mrs Ruffner and Hampton had taught him.

Booker also started a small reading room, where people could come to read papers, and a debating society for young men. On Sundays he taught in two Sunday schools, so he was busy from morning until night.
Booker was proud to help his brothers John and James go to Hampton, and he sent other good pupils there as well. He knew how much the school had changed his own life, and he wanted the same for them.

These were the years of Reconstruction, when Black men voted and held public office for the first time. Politics was the talk of every town, and many people hoped that the vote alone would solve all their problems.

Booker noticed that some people thought a degree in Latin or Greek was a way to escape hard work. He believed in learning, but he began to wonder what kind of education would truly help his people to live better.
In 1878 Booker felt that he still had much to learn, so he went to Washington to study at Wayland Seminary. It was the first time that he had lived in a great city.
In Washington he saw some young men who spent their money on fine clothes and fancy carriages while they waited for government jobs. He thought they would have done better to learn useful skills.
For a while Booker wondered whether he should become a minister, because many educated young men chose that road. He did not decide anything yet, and he went on studying and thinking.
Near the end of the school year, a letter arrived from General Armstrong. He invited Booker to come back to Hampton in June 1879 and speak to the graduating class.
Booker worked on the speech with great care, and when he stood up before the crowd in the hall, it went well. His confidence grew, and he was glad to be back at the school that had made him.
After the speech the General offered Booker a place on the teaching staff. He would look after a group of Native American students and also begin a night school for poor workers.

Dozens of young Native Americans had come to Hampton from the western plains, and they lived in a dormitory called the Wigwam. Booker lived there with them as their house father, and he was proud that the General trusted him.

The students came from different nations, and most of them spoke very little English. Booker taught them patiently, but he knew that the changes in clothes, food and habits at Hampton were hard for them.

Many poor students could not pay for school, so they worked all day in the shops and the fields at Hampton. Booker started a night school for them, and they were called the Plucky Class because they studied after a day of hard work.

The night students were tired, but they worked harder than anyone, and Booker admired their courage. General Armstrong trusted him more and more, and Booker was so happy at Hampton that he thought he would stay there for life.

In Tuskegee, Alabama, a skilled tinsmith named Lewis Adams, who had once been enslaved, wanted a school for Black children. A white businessman, George Campbell, wanted the same thing, and the two men worked together.
Historians say that Adams helped to win Black votes for a candidate who promised a school. After the election, the state agreed to pay two thousand dollars a year for the teachers of a new school.
Adams and Campbell wrote to General Armstrong at Hampton to ask for a principal. They expected him to send a white man, because they could not imagine that a Black man would run such a school.
Armstrong wrote back that he knew of no white man he could recommend. He said that he knew a young Black teacher at Hampton who might be the right person, and that his name was Booker Washington.
A few days later, a telegram came from Tuskegee saying that Booker Washington would suit them and should be sent at once. Booker was surprised, because he had never thought of running a school.
Booker was about twenty-five, and he had never been in charge of a school before. He was proud, but he was also afraid, and he thanked General Armstrong for trusting him.
In June 1881 Booker took the train south into Alabama, and he looked out of the window all the way. He did not know what he would find at the end of the journey.

Tuskegee lay in the Black Belt, a region named for its dark, rich soil and for the large Black population that lived there. In that part of Alabama there were many more Black families than white families.
When Booker arrived, he looked around for the school and found that it did not exist. There was no land, no building and no equipment, and the state had promised money only for teachers.

The only places that the people of the town could offer him were an old church called Butler Chapel and a poor shanty beside it. Booker looked at them and decided that, small as they were, they would have to do.
Before the school opened, Booker travelled the countryside for a month by cart. He wanted to see how the people lived, and what they would need from a school.
He went into many one-room cabins, where whole families slept in a single room. The meals were often pork and cornbread, and there was little else on the table.
In one cabin Booker saw an expensive organ that no one in the family could play. They had bought it on credit, and now they owed money for something they could not use.
He saw that many farmers rented their land and bought food and tools on credit from the store. At harvest time they gave most of their crop to pay the debt, and then they started all over again.
The little country schools opened for only a few months of each year, and their buildings were poor. There were few books, and the teachers had often had very little education themselves.
Booker talked with farmers over the fence and sat in their cabins at dinner. He decided that his school would have to teach people how to live, farm and build, as well as how to read.
On 4 July 1881, the school opened in the old church and the poor little house beside it. Booker was the only teacher, and he had very little furniture and almost no books.
About thirty students came on the first day, and most of them were grown men and women. Many were already teachers, but they wanted to know more, so they sat down in the old church and began.
Booker found that his students knew much from books, but that some did not know how to keep clean. He told them all to bathe, to keep their beds tidy and to buy and use a toothbrush.
Soon afterwards a young teacher named Olivia Davidson arrived. She had studied at Hampton and in Massachusetts, and she was able and full of energy.
The little school soon needed more room, and an old plantation of about a hundred acres was for sale near the town. It cost more than Booker had, but he thought it was exactly what the school needed.
Booker wrote to General Marshall, the treasurer at Hampton, and asked for a loan. The money arrived soon afterwards, and five hundred dollars made the first payment on the land.
The land had been worn out by years of cotton, and the big house had burned down long ago. Only a poor kitchen, a stable and a hen-house were still standing among the weeds.

Many students did not like the idea of working on the land, because they had come to Tuskegee to study. Some of them had hoped that education would free them from farm work for ever, and they said so.
Booker answered by taking an axe in his own hands and starting to clear the bushes. When the students saw their principal working in old clothes, they came to join him, and the work began.
For weeks the students cut down bushes, burned the piles and dug out the roots. It was hard work in the summer heat, but little by little the old fields began to look like farmland again.
When the ground was ready, the students ploughed it and planted crops of vegetables and corn. The harvest would help to feed the school, and the students learned farming by doing it.
The old kitchen, the stable and the hen-house were scrubbed clean and turned into rooms for lessons and work. They were poor places, but there was now more room than there had been in the church.
Miss Davidson was good at raising money, and she organised suppers and festivals in the town. Black and white neighbours came to them, and every dollar they raised was used for the school.

There were many nights when Booker could not sleep, because the school had debts and payments to make. In the morning he saw the students at work and the help of kind neighbours, and he found fresh courage.

The old kitchen and the hen-house were not enough for the growing school, and Booker wanted a proper building. He decided that the students would make the bricks themselves, so that they would learn a trade and save money.
They dug red clay from the school's land, pressed it into wooden moulds and left the soft bricks in rows to dry. The trouble was that no one at Tuskegee knew how to burn them properly.
They stacked the dry bricks into a great kiln and lit the fires, but something went wrong. When they opened it, most of the bricks were spoiled, and weeks of work were wasted.
They tried again with a second kiln, but this one failed as well. Some people said that the school should give up, and many of the students were tired and discouraged.
Booker did not want to give up, but the school had no money for another try. He took his watch to a pawnbroker, borrowed fifteen dollars on it, and used the money to start a third kiln.
This time the students tended the fires day and night, and Booker shared the anxious watch. Nobody dared to sleep for long, because one mistake might ruin everything again.
When at last the kiln had cooled, the students opened it carefully and looked inside. The bricks were good and strong, and a great cheer went up from everyone who was watching.
Soon the school was selling bricks to people in the town, and the brickyard brought in useful money. It also gave the students a chance to learn a trade that was needed all over the South.
The students who learned to make bricks could now earn a living with a skill that they could use anywhere. Booker saw that when a student learned by doing real work, he learned twice as well.
With good bricks at last, Booker could plan the school's first large building. The students dug a deep trench for the foundation, and they were proud to be building their own school.
A friend of the school in Brooklyn, Mr Porter, sent a gift of money for a new building. It was the first large building that Tuskegee would have, and it was named Porter Hall in his honour.
The students laid the walls with the bricks they had made themselves. They learned the work of a bricklayer as they went along, one row at a time.
Other students worked in the carpentry shop, cutting wood and building doors and window frames. They were learning a trade, and at the same time they were making real parts of a real house.
Lumber, nails and glass cost money, and Booker was always close to running out. He paid each bill as soon as he could, because he wanted the school to have a good name.
Week by week the walls grew higher, and the whole school came out to watch. The students felt that the building belonged to them, because they had made it from the ground up.
At last Porter Hall was finished, and it was a fine building with classrooms and rooms for living. The students were proud to walk into it, because they knew that they had built it themselves.
There were no beds in the new building, so the students made their own, with cloth and straw for the mattresses. They joked that they had to make their beds before they could lie on them.

Booker wanted the school to teach daily life as well as lessons, so he asked for proper tables, cloths and plates at every meal. Many students had never eaten like that, and they learned how with some laughter.
In 1882 Booker married Fannie Smith, a young woman from Malden whom he had known for years. She came to live at the school and helped him in his work.
The following year their daughter Portia was born, and the little family was very happy. Sadly, Fannie died about two years after the wedding, and Booker went back to his work with a heavy heart.
Olivia Davidson travelled north again and again to ask for help for the school. She had weak health, but she was cheerful and clever, and she returned with gifts.
After some years Booker and Olivia were married, and they had two sons. She went on working for the school while she cared for the boys, and she gave all her strength to both.
In 1889 Olivia died, worn out by years of work and illness. The whole school was in mourning, and Booker lost a wife and the teacher who had done more than anyone to help him.
That same year Margaret Murray, a graduate of Fisk University, came to Tuskegee to be the Lady Principal. She was strong and capable, and she took charge of the girls' education.
Warren Logan, a Hampton graduate, came to Tuskegee and became the school's treasurer. Like the other teachers, he worked for very little money, because he believed in the school.
In the evenings, the students gathered in the chapel for prayers and sang the old spirituals that their parents had known. The singing became a loved tradition, and visitors never forgot it.
