On his travels Booker was sometimes refused a hotel room or a seat on a train because he was Black. He did not answer with anger, because he had decided that he would never let himself hate anyone.
Booker often walked around the campus and visited the students' rooms himself. He believed that small things, such as a swept path or a made bed, showed the true spirit of a school.
Every student at Tuskegee had to work with his hands each day, in the fields, the shops or the kitchens. The work paid a part of the cost of his education, and it also taught him a trade.
As at Hampton, there was a night school for students who could not pay the full fees. They worked all day for the school, and in the evening they went to class with tired eyes and strong hearts.
The school needed money for land, buildings and teachers, and Booker could not find enough in Alabama. So he spent many months each year travelling north by train to ask for help.
He spoke in churches and in the parlours of private homes. He did not beg, but told the plain story of the school and let people decide for themselves.

Booker kept honest accounts and could show exactly what had been done with every gift. He invited donors to visit Tuskegee, because he believed that people give more freely when they can see the results.
Many doors stayed closed, and many people gave him nothing at all. Booker went away politely and often came back the next year, and he never allowed himself to be discouraged.
One day an old woman named Aunt Caroline Smith, who was very poor and who had once been enslaved, came to the school. She had no money, but she gave six eggs, and Booker never forgot her gift.
Booker wrote a letter of thanks to every person who gave, whether the gift was large or small. He believed that gratitude should be shown clearly, and that kindness should be answered with kindness.
Gradually, people from the North came south to visit the school. They saw the students at work in the fields and the shops, and many of them left as friends of Tuskegee.
A fund called the Slater Fund had been set up to help the education of freed people. In later years it gave grants to Tuskegee that helped to pay the teachers.

The travelling was exhausting, because Booker rode night trains and waited in cold stations. Yet each long journey brought money or friends, and every dollar meant a little more room for the students.
As gifts came in from the North, new buildings began to rise beside Porter Hall. The students made the bricks and built the walls, and the school grew a little each year.

Year by year, Tuskegee added more and more trades to its list of lessons. Students could now learn carpentry, blacksmithing, printing, shoemaking, harness making and tailoring, and most of them worked on real jobs for the school.
In 1892 Robert Taylor, a trained Black architect, came to teach at Tuskegee. He drew the plans for many new buildings, and the students built them.
Booker wanted to help the farmers of the area, so he invited them to a meeting at Tuskegee. He thought that neighbours who talked about their problems might find answers together.
In February 1892 about four hundred men and women came to the first Tuskegee Negro Conference. Some of them had never been inside a school, and they travelled by wagon and mule from all around.

Booker asked the farmers plain questions: did they own their land, did they owe money, and did their families live in one room? The farmers answered honestly, and many of them were surprised by their own answers.

One by one, the farmers stood up and spoke about their debts, their rents and the crops that gave the best return. They had never before been asked for their views, and they spoke with great frankness.
The farmers went home with practical ideas about saving money, buying land and building better houses. The conference became a yearly event, and the idea soon spread to other parts of the South.
General Armstrong had been ill for some time, and in 1893 he died. Booker was deeply sad, because he had lost the man who had been his teacher, his example and his friend.
Armstrong was buried at Hampton, among the students he had loved. Booker thought about all that he had learned from the General, and he promised himself that he would carry on his work.
In 1893 Booker married Margaret Murray, who had been Lady Principal of the school since 1889. She became his steady partner, and she led the school's work for women with great skill.

In 1895 the city of Atlanta planned a great fair, called the Cotton States and International Exposition, to show how the South was growing. It included a special building to show the work of Black Americans.
Some time before, Booker had spoken in Washington to a committee of Congress, in support of the fair. The men from Atlanta who heard him were impressed by his calm, honest way of speaking.
The directors of the Exposition invited Booker to speak at the opening ceremony. He knew that it was a great honour, and he accepted, although he was also very nervous.

Booker knew that he had two audiences, one Black and one white, and that both were watching him. Black listeners feared that he would say too little, and many white listeners feared that he would say too much.
He wrote the speech with great care, crossing out words and writing them again. He wanted to say what was true, and he also wanted to win the goodwill of everyone who heard him.
The teachers and students at Tuskegee wished him luck and waved as his train pulled away. Booker hardly slept on the journey, because his mind was full of the speech.
On the opening day, the streets of Atlanta were full of banners, bands and crowds. The sun was hot, and thousands of people were walking toward the Exposition grounds.

Booker sat on a high platform among governors and Southern leaders, as one of the first Black men to speak at such an event. He later said that his heart was beating so loudly that he could hardly hear himself.
Governor Rufus Bullock stood up to introduce him to the great hall. He called Booker a representative of Negro civilisation, and the crowd applauded.
A hush fell over the hall as Booker stood up. In a clear, steady voice, he began by reminding everyone that a third of the people of the South were Black.
Booker told the crowd that one third of the South was Black, and that no plan for the future could ignore these people. He said that the two races would rise or fall together.
Then he told a story about a ship that was lost at sea for many days. The sailors begged another ship for water, but the answer was always the same: “Cast down your bucket where you are.”
The thirsty captain heard the same answer again and again, and at last he obeyed. His bucket came up full of fresh, sweet water, because the ship was at the mouth of the Amazon River.

Booker told his Black listeners to cast down their bucket where they were, in farming, trades, housework and business. He asked them to do their work well and to make themselves useful to the people around them.

Then he spoke to the white listeners and asked them to look to the neighbours who had worked their fields and built their railroads. These were people they already knew, and he asked them to give them a fair chance.
He held up his hand and said that in social matters the races could be as separate as the fingers. But in everything that helped all to progress, he said, they could be as one hand.
Booker also said that no people could rise until they learned that farming a field is as dignified as writing a poem. The idea was simple, but many people in the hall remembered it for years.
When he finished, the crowd rose and cheered, and men and women waved their hats and handkerchiefs. Governor Bullock hurried across the platform and shook his hand, and the cheering went on and on.
Within a day or two, newspapers all over the country printed parts of the speech. President Grover Cleveland sent him a letter of thanks, and Booker's name was known across America.

Not everyone approved, and some Black leaders said that Booker had given up too much on voting rights and equal treatment. Booker believed that his plan was the wisest road, and the argument has gone on ever since.
In 1896 Harvard University gave Booker a special honorary degree. It was a rare honour for a Black American at that time, and it showed how far his reputation had grown.

That same year George Washington Carver, a trained scientist who had been born into slavery, came to Tuskegee to teach agriculture. Booker had warned him that there would be hard work and little money.

Carver set up a laboratory with very simple things, and he taught farmers how to rest worn-out soil. He showed them that crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes could help the land, and he wrote simple bulletins for them.

Booker had learned a lot about speaking in public, and he shared his ideas with students. He said that a speaker should have something to say, forget himself and talk plainly and warmly to his listeners.
In October 1898 Booker spoke at a peace celebration in Chicago, with the President sitting nearby. He praised the Black soldiers who had fought in the war with Spain, and the audience cheered.
In December 1898 President William McKinley visited Tuskegee, and several members of his cabinet came with him. The whole school came out to greet them, and the students stood in long lines.
The visitors watched the students at work in the classrooms, the shops and the fields. McKinley said kind words about the school, and Booker felt that its work was now known to the whole country.
By 1899 Booker was worn out by years of travelling, speaking and raising money. His friends urged him to rest, and they helped to pay for a trip to Europe, where he sailed with his wife.
In Europe, Booker was treated with courtesy in hotels and on the street, and he found it a welcome change. He visited several countries, met interesting people and saw how ordinary workers lived.
Booker came home rested and grateful, and the students cheered when he stepped off the train. He had many new ideas for the school, and he was soon busy again.
In 1900 Booker founded the National Negro Business League in Boston. He wanted Black business owners to meet and learn from each other, and to prove that they could succeed.
The League soon had branches in many towns, and shop owners, farmers and bankers shared their ideas. Booker believed that every successful business was a small victory for the whole community.
Booker told his life story in a series of chapters for a magazine in 1900. He had help from friends and editors, but the voice was his own, simple and honest and often funny.

In 1901 the chapters were published together as a book called Up From Slavery. It became very popular, and it was later translated into many languages, so that readers all over the world could follow his journey.
In October 1901 President Theodore Roosevelt asked Booker to dinner at the White House. Many white Southerners were angry, but Black Americans and many Northerners saw it as a sign of respect.
Roosevelt sometimes asked Booker for his advice, and Booker's influence grew. So did the number of his critics, who thought he had too much power and too much patience.

In 1903 W E B Du Bois wrote a book that criticised Booker's approach as too slow. Later, in 1909, a group of people formed a new organisation that wanted a faster and more direct fight for equal rights.
By 1915 Booker was ill and worn out, and he collapsed while visiting New York. He asked to be taken home to Tuskegee, and he died there on 14 November, aged about fifty-nine.
Thousands of people came to honour him at his funeral. He was buried on the campus, close to the red brick buildings that his students had made with their own hands.
Tuskegee is now a university, and part of its campus is a national historic site where visitors can learn about Booker's life. His book is still read, and people still argue about his ideas.
C1C2: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery on a small farm in Franklin County, Virginia, most probably in 1856, although he himself believed it was a year or two later. Like most children of the enslaved, he never learned his exact birthday, and of his white father he knew nothing at all. In the book he wrote as a grown man, he begins his story with these uncertain, humble facts.

Booker's earliest home was a crude log cabin that also served as the farm's kitchen, where his mother, Jane, cooked for the white family. It had a dirt floor, a hole for the cat to come and go, and a pit in one corner where sweet potatoes were stored for the winter. Glass windows were an unknown luxury, and in cold weather the wind whistled freely through the cracks.

Because there was no stove, Jane prepared every meal for the farm over an open fireplace, in the heat of summer and the dark of winter alike. Her work began before dawn and often continued long after the family in the big house had gone to bed. Her small son grew up in the smoke and the glow of that fire, watching a woman who never seemed to rest.

The children had no beds, and they slept on a heap of rags spread on the cold earth of the floor. They had no table either, and nobody ever called them to a family meal: a scrap of bread was snatched here, a cup of milk there, and a roasted potato wherever one could be found. He later said it was more like the feeding of animals than a family meal, and he never forgot that.

Booker was not alone in that hard place, for he had an older brother, John, and a sister, Amanda, who shared everything he owned, which was almost nothing. The three children played in the dust of the farmyard and kept close together, as small creatures do when the world around them is unkind. Their mother had little time for them, but her love gave the cabin a warmth that the fireplace alone could not.

For clothing, the slave children received a single shirt of coarse flax, and Booker found it the cruelest garment ever invented, since the rough, uncut fibres pricked his skin like a hundred pins. His brother John, who was somewhat older, offered to wear the shirt first until its sharpest edges were worn smooth. Booker remembered it long afterwards as one of the kindest acts of his childhood.

In winter the children were given stiff, heavy shoes with wooden soles and leather tops, which clattered on every hard floor and were miserable to walk in. Even so, he reflected later, such small hardships were nothing beside the larger wrong of being owned like a horse or a cow. Booker had little else to keep out the cold, and the winters seemed very long to a small boy in a house with no glass.

As a small boy Booker was sent to the mill, some distance away, with a bag of corn thrown across the back of a horse, and the load was always a worry. On one journey the sack slid to the ground, and being far too small to hoist it back, he sat beside the road and waited, frightened, for a stranger to pass. The mill trips were a lonely duty, and they showed him how much even a small child was made to carry.

One of his lighter tasks was to carry the books of his young mistress to the schoolhouse, and he walked behind her, proud and silent, along the dusty lane. Through the open door he glimpsed a room full of boys and girls bent over their lessons, and the sight pierced him with longing. To be allowed to sit among them, he thought, would be the nearest thing to heaven that a boy could imagine.

Even in the cabin, the enslaved people of the farm knew that a great war was being fought, because news travelled among them by whispers, which they called the grapevine telegraph. Booker woke one night to find his mother kneeling over him in the dark, praying quietly that President Lincoln and his army might succeed. The scene taught him that freedom was something people could hope for and ask God to bring.

As the war dragged on, the effects were felt even on a modest farm like the one where Booker lived, for coffee, sugar and manufactured goods grew scarcer with each passing month. The enslaved people, who were supposed to know nothing, followed every battle through the grapevine telegraph and read the faces of their owners for signs of defeat. Hope, which had flickered for years like a small flame in the dark, was now a steady and growing light.

Early in the spring of 1865, the people of the farm were summoned to the front of the big house, where a stranger, who seemed to Booker to be an officer of the Union, read aloud a long and solemn paper. The boy was too young to follow its legal phrases, but he understood the meaning at once, because the faces of the grown people around him told him everything. He believed it was the Emancipation Proclamation, which had at last reached their corner of Virginia.

His mother, who had been so quiet and so strong for so long, bent down and kissed each of her children, and her cheeks were wet with tears of joy. She told them that Abraham Lincoln and the Union army were the cause of this day, and that it was the day for which she had prayed through all those dark nights. Booker never forgot the sight, and the picture of that morning, with its tears and its trembling joy, stayed with him for the rest of his life.

Booker is honest about what followed, for the first gladness was soon replaced by something like gloom, and he calls this the strange part of freedom. Families who had worked their whole lives for nothing now had no land, no money and no roofs of their own, and several elderly people lingered at the old gate because they had nowhere else to go. Freedom, it turned out, was a gift that had to be earned a second time.

Freedom brought many quiet changes, and one of the strangest was that people who had been known by a single name now had to settle on a second one. Families sat for hours deliberating, some inclined towards the name of a celebrated statesman, others towards that of their former owner, and some towards an invention entirely their own. To choose a name, Booker later understood, was to take the first step into a new life.

Booker's stepfather, Washington Ferguson, had already gone to Malden, in West Virginia, where he had found work among the salt furnaces, and he now sent word that his family should join him. Everything they owned, a few pots, some blankets and a little bedding, was packed into a wagon, and the little party set off at dawn. The boy looked back only once at the cabin where he had been born.

The journey to West Virginia took many days, because the road climbed over hills and wound through forests, and the mother and her children took turns to walk beside the wagon. They stopped each evening to cook over a fire by the roadside, and slept in the open under the stars. For Booker, who had never been more than a few miles from home, every bend in the road was an adventure.

Malden, when they reached it, was a rough and crowded town squeezed into a valley by a river, where the furnaces boiled brine day and night and a grey smoke lay over the roofs. The family's new cabin stood in a poor and noisy corner of the settlement, among people who drank, gambled and quarrelled, and Booker thought it worse than the farm they had left. It was a long way from the free and shining life that he had imagined on the road.

Almost at once Ferguson arranged for the two boys to work in the salt furnace, where they shovelled and packed the dry white crystals into barrels, and they had to be at their places by four in the morning. Booker was only about nine years old, and the long hours in the heat and the dust left him tired to the bone. Yet he was learning that a boy who is free to work is also free to hope.

Every barrel that left the furnace was stamped with the number of the man who had packed it, and Booker's stepfather was number eighteen. The boy copied the figure over and over, with a stub of chalk on the barrel tops, until he could make the two shapes by himself without help. It was a modest start, but he had never forgotten the longing to read that had first stirred in him outside the schoolhouse door.

Booker's mother, who could neither read nor write, somehow obtained a copy of the famous blue-backed spelling book and put it into his hands. By the light of the fire he studied the alphabet, tracing each letter with his finger, and with no teacher but his own stubbornness he mastered it. It was a remarkable victory for a boy who had been told, in effect, that books were not for people like him.

News soon spread through the settlement that a young Black teacher from Ohio had arrived to open a school, and the excitement was extraordinary, as if a great guest had come to town. In the custom of the place, he lived with each family in turn for a week, and every household offered the best food it could afford. Booker watched the stranger with something close to awe, for he seemed to carry the whole world in his schoolbag.

Booker begged his stepfather to let him go to school, but Ferguson, who needed every dollar the boys could earn at the furnace, would not hear of it. The refusal was a cruel disappointment, and Booker later admitted that he had never wanted anything more. For some time the schoolhouse remained a place that he could only look at from outside.

Eventually a compromise was found, and Booker was allowed to attend a night school and then, later, the day school itself, provided that he worked before the lessons began and again in the afternoon. He arrived tired and often late, with the dust of the furnace still on his hands, yet he sat down with a hunger that his classmates found hard to match. Every hour in the classroom had been paid for with an hour of labour.

On his first day at school, the teacher called the roll and asked each pupil for his full name, and Booker realised with alarm that he had only one. He had never needed a second, since on the farm everyone knew him as Booker, but a boy at school evidently needed a surname. With perfect composure he answered Washington, as though he had carried the name since the day of his birth.

Some time afterwards he discovered that his mother had in fact named him Booker Taliaferro soon after he was born, although the second name had never been used in the slave quarters. He promptly restored it, writing Taliaferro between Booker and Washington, and it pleased him that his real name had been waiting for him all those years. Few men, he reflected, choose a name so well on the spur of the moment.

The boys at school wore caps bought in a shop, and Booker, who had none, felt his poverty acutely until his mother stepped in. She took two pieces of homespun cloth, stitched them together and handed him the result, and he wore it into the schoolroom without a flicker of embarrassment. It taught him an early and valuable lesson: that the opinion of others about one's clothes counts for very little.

His mother's generosity was larger than her means, and she adopted a young orphan named James, who had nobody to care for him, and raised him with her own children. The little cabin was already full to bursting, but she never allowed hardship to harden her heart. Booker saw in her an example of quiet charity that he remembered for the rest of his life.

For a time Booker was put to work in a coal mine, where the narrow tunnels were as black as midnight and the damp air clung to his skin. He was always frightened that he would lose his way or that a roof might fall, and the fear stayed with him long after he left. The mine was one more school of hard experience, though he would gladly have exchanged it for a real one.

It was in the darkness of the coal mine that Booker overheard two miners discussing a wonderful school for Black students called Hampton Institute, hundreds of miles away in Virginia. They explained that poor young people could work there to pay for their board and receive an education, and the thought lodged in the boy's mind like a seed. He resolved, there and then, that he would go to Hampton, whatever it cost him.

Booker's employers at the salt furnace and the coal mine were General Lewis Ruffner and his wife, Viola, a native of Vermont who had a formidable reputation in the town. She was known as a woman of exacting standards, and it was said that no boy had ever stayed long in her household because nothing he did could satisfy her. For a boy of Booker's age, the prospect of working in her house was frightening indeed.

Booker had heard about the many boys who had failed in her service, and he took the post with a trembling heart, hoping against hope that he would last longer than they had. He needed the wages, and he also sensed that the household of a woman so careful about everything might teach him a great deal. His first days in the big house were an ordeal of nerves, and he scarcely dared to breathe.

Mrs Ruffner expected the house to be spotless from attic to cellar, every article returned to its proper place and every task completed on the hour, and she moved from room to room like an inspector. Nothing escaped her notice, from a smear on a window to a latch left unfastened, and she spoke her mind without anger but also without compromise. To a boy raised in a one-room cabin, it was a bewildering new world.

When Booker swept a yard or scrubbed a floor, she would examine the work closely and send him back if the smallest flaw remained, and he was often compelled to repeat a job several times. At first he thought it harsh, but he gradually perceived that she was not being unkind, only determined that he should do things properly. He learned, to his own surprise, to take pride in a task that was truly and completely finished.

In the winter months, Mrs Ruffner allowed him to attend school for a few hours each day, provided that every household duty had first been completed to her satisfaction. Booker rose early, worked with speed and care, and hurried to the schoolhouse with the happiest feeling in the world. The bargain taught him to use every minute well, since each one was precious to him.

Mrs Ruffner soon noticed how eager the boy was to read, and she did something that he never forgot: she encouraged him to study in his spare moments and treated his ambition as something worth respecting. For the first time in his life, a person with power over him was cheering him on instead of holding him back. Her kindness, hidden behind such a stern manner, taught him never to judge a person by the surface alone.

He remained in her service for about a year and a half, and in that time she taught him the habits that he would later regard as the foundations of his character: cleanliness, punctuality and strict honesty. He observed that these were the very qualities that the poor most needed to win the respect of their neighbours. Years afterwards, he insisted on them at Tuskegee with the same determination she had shown.

The deepest lesson of all was that no task is truly done until it is done thoroughly, and that a person who works well when unobserved has already won an important victory. Booker admitted that he had often resented her inspections in those early weeks, but he came to see them as a form of respect, since she demanded his best because she believed he could give it. It was a standard that he would apply to himself and others for the rest of his life.

All the while, the memory of the miners' conversation never left him, and the dream of Hampton grew stronger with every passing month, as he laid aside each spare coin with painful care. His mother, who understood what the school meant to him, was nevertheless anxious about letting her son travel so far from home on so little money. She wavered for a long time, but in the end she could not bring herself to stand in his way.

In 1872, when Booker was about sixteen years old, he packed a few clothes into a small, cheap bag and prepared to begin the long journey to Hampton, hundreds of miles away. Many of the old and poor people of the neighbourhood, who had little to spare, came to the door and pressed nickels and quarters into his hand, and he accepted every coin with gratitude. He carried their faith with him along the road more surely than any luggage.

Booker said goodbye to his mother, his brother and the neighbours who had gathered at the door, and he set out for Hampton with a small, cheap bag and a heart full of hope. The school lay hundreds of miles away in Virginia, and he had only a vague idea of the road. Whatever lay ahead, he had made up his mind that he would not turn back.

For part of the journey he rode in a stagecoach, winding up through the mountains, but the fare soon swallowed what little money he had. When it was gone, he went on foot, begging a ride from any wagon driver who would take him, and walking whenever nobody would. Each mile that he covered on his own feet was a small victory over his tiredness and his fear of failing.

On the road, he arrived at a roadside inn one night, weary and cold, and asked for a bed, but he was refused because he was Black. It was one of his first direct encounters with the colour line, and he met it without self-pity, though it was a bitter pill after so many days of walking. He spent that night out in the open, with nothing to keep him warm but his own stubborn determination to go on.

At last, tired, hungry and ragged, Booker reached Richmond, the Virginia capital, long after dark, with not a single penny in his pocket and not a single friend in the city. The noise and the lights of the streets were bewildering to a country boy, and there was nobody to whom he could turn. He walked for hours through the unfamiliar streets, uncertain where to go and too proud to beg for help.

Finding no place that would take him in, Booker noticed that the wooden sidewalk in one street stood raised above the ground, and he crept beneath it and lay down. All night he heard the footsteps of strangers passing overhead, and, exhausted though he was, he slept better than he had expected. It was an unusual bedroom for a future founder of a school, but at least it kept the wind and the rain away from him.

The next morning Booker was desperately hungry, and when he saw a ship being unloaded at the water's edge, he went up to the captain, a white man, and asked whether he might work. The captain kindly allowed him to carry heavy loads of iron for several days, and he earned enough to buy food and to continue. Booker never forgot the stranger's generosity, and he remembered it with gratitude for the rest of his life.

Having scraped together a few coins, Booker pressed on towards Hampton, and when at last he came in sight of the school's large brick buildings, the effect on him was electrical. He had never seen such grand and solid walls, built for the education of people like himself, and he felt that he had reached the promised land. All the miles, all the hunger and all the loneliness of the road seemed suddenly worth the price that he had paid.

He knew very well, however, that he was a sorry spectacle: his clothes were filthy, his shoes were worn and his face was streaked with the dirt of the road. The head teacher, Miss Mary Mackie, spoke with other applicants and said hardly a word to him, and as the hours passed, he began to fear that he would be turned away. He stood and waited, as quietly as he could, with all the patience that years of hard work had taught him.

At last, Miss Mackie turned to him and said that the recitation room next door needed sweeping, and she handed him a broom. Booker understood at once that this was his entrance examination, and he was delighted, because it was a kind of test that he knew he could pass. He remembered every lesson that Mrs Ruffner had ever taught him, and he resolved to prove that none of them had been wasted.

He swept the room three times, moved every table and bench, cleaned every closet and corner, and then took a cloth and dusted the furniture four times over. Miss Mackie came in, drew her handkerchief across the woodwork and the floor, and found not a single speck of dirt, whereupon she said quietly that she thought he would do for the school. He remarked years later that he would give more for the memory of that simple test than for any diploma that he ever received.

Having passed the sweeping test, Booker was given a place at Hampton, and since he had nothing with which to pay, the school made him a janitor in return for his board. His duties were to rise before dawn to light the fires, to sweep and dust the classrooms and to keep everything in order. He performed each one with the same thoroughness that he had learned from Mrs Ruffner, and he never once arrived late.

That first night he was shown to a dormitory bed with two white sheets, and, never having owned even one, he was thoroughly puzzled about what to do with them. On the first night he slept beneath both sheets, and on the second he lay on top of both, until he finally watched the other boys and understood. He tells the story with a good-humoured smile at his own ignorance, and he asks his readers to smile with him.

The principal of Hampton was General Samuel Chapman Armstrong, who had been born in Hawaii, the son of missionaries, and had commanded a regiment of Black soldiers in the Civil War before founding the school in 1868. Booker looked up to him with a reverence that bordered on worship, and he declared that he had never met a man so noble in character or so unselfish in purpose. The General's example, both in his courage and in his plain, unselfish way of living, was to shape his entire career.

The lesson that Armstrong returned to again and again, in chapel and in conversation, was that the happiest people in the world are those who do the most to make others useful and happy. It was an unfamiliar thought to a boy who had been taught for years to look after nothing but himself and his family. Booker took it into his heart, and it would become the quiet engine of everything he built.

Hampton operated rather like a military camp, with bells marking every hour, uniforms for the students, drill on the lawn and strict inspections of rooms and clothing. For some students such discipline was a burden, but Booker, who had grown up in chaos and want, found it a deep and unexpected comfort. He understood now that order was not the enemy of freedom but the foundation of it.

Alongside their books, the students were required to learn a trade and to work with their hands, whether in carpentry, farming, tailoring, printing or housework. Booker, who had once believed that education was a way of escaping labour, saw instead young men and women who took real pride in a well-made shoe or a well-swept floor. It was the first time that he understood how work could ennoble a person rather than diminish him.

Although Booker could not afford his fees, General Armstrong arranged for a generous benefactor in Massachusetts to pay them on his behalf, and he accepted the gift with a mixture of gratitude and awe. He had never met the man at that time, and he made up his mind to repay the kindness by working harder than anyone else. He considered it a debt of honour, and he never lost sight of the fact that someone far away believed in him.

One of Booker's teachers, Miss Nathalie Lord, took a special interest in training him to read aloud and to speak with clarity, and she held him to the highest standard. She taught him that a voice, like any other skill, could be improved by patient practice, and that every word deserves to be given its full meaning. Her influence would be felt in the great speeches of his later life, long after he had left her classroom.

Beyond the classroom, Booker joined the school's debating society, where the students gathered each week to argue about politics, religion and the problems of the day. He was nervous at first, afraid of making a fool of himself, but gradually he discovered that he had a gift for stating an argument clearly and persuading his listeners. These weekly meetings were his first real training in the art of public speaking, and he valued them for the rest of his career.

Since Hampton gave him room and instruction but little pocket money, Booker had to find work every summer, and he took whatever jobs he could to pay his debts and buy what he needed. He worked long hours in the heat, saved what he could and went back to Hampton each autumn hungry for the next year of study. The pattern of work and learning would serve him for the rest of his life.

In 1875, after three years of unremitting study and labour, Booker graduated from Hampton, and the boy who had once packed salt in the dark now held a diploma in his hand. He had walked hundreds of miles, slept under a sidewalk and swept a room three times to arrive at this day, and the achievement filled him with wonder. It was not the end of his education, however, but the beginning of his duty to others.

When he returned to Malden, the whole neighbourhood turned out to welcome him, and his mother, his brothers and his old friends crowded around to hear about the great school beyond the mountains. For many of them, Hampton was a name in a story, and the young man who had actually been there seemed to bring a breath of the wider world. Booker was moved by their pride in him, and a little humbled by how much they expected of him now.

The Black families of Malden had a great longing for schooling, and they soon asked their returned son to take charge of the local school, which he did with a sense of joy and responsibility. The community plainly wished to see one of its own children succeed, and the offer was made with real warmth. Booker accepted at once, because he longed to give back what Hampton had so freely given to him.

In the day school the children came in every size, from small ones who could scarcely hold a pencil to tall boys and girls who had already worked in the furnaces, and there were very few books to go round. Booker taught reading, writing and arithmetic by every means he could invent, and he insisted on good manners as well as correct answers. The little schoolroom was crowded and noisy, and he loved every minute of it.

At night the school opened its doors again for the men and women who had laboured for twelve hours in the furnaces and the mines, and many of them were old enough to be Booker's grandparents. They came in their working clothes, tired to the bone, and bent over their primers with a fierce determination to read the Bible for themselves. Seeing their hunger for knowledge only deepened his faith in the power of education to change a life.

Booker believed that lessons in cleanliness were as important as lessons in grammar, so he taught his pupils to wash their hands and faces, comb their hair, keep their clothes tidy and look after their teeth. Some of them found these habits strange at first, but they soon came to feel the difference in their self-respect. He was applying, in a rough schoolroom in West Virginia, everything that Mrs Ruffner and General Armstrong had taught him.

Outside the classroom he was equally busy, for he opened a small reading room where people could come in to read the newspapers, and he started a debating society for the young men of the town. On Sundays he taught in two separate Sunday schools, and he was seldom to be found with an idle hour. He thought of it all as repayment of a debt that he could never quite settle.

Nothing pleased Booker more than seeing other young people follow his path, and he did all he could to help his brothers John and James go to Hampton, and to find money for several promising pupils as well. He knew from his own experience how much the school could change a life, and he wished the same chance for them. Few of his early duties gave him more pleasure than packing a hopeful pupil off to the school that had changed his own life.

These were the years of Reconstruction, when Black men for the first time voted and held public office, and politics became the passion of every town in the South, including Malden. Many people hoped that the ballot alone would solve every problem, and meetings and speeches filled the evenings, while the Ku Klux Klan terrorised Black families in other parts of the region. Booker watched it all closely, with a mixture of hope, caution and some doubt.

Booker noticed that a number of people around him seemed to think that a degree in Latin or Greek was a ticket to a life without manual work, and that political office was a sure road to success. He believed deeply in learning, yet he began to wonder what sort of education would truly help his people to live better, to earn more and to stand on their own feet. The question would occupy his thoughts for the rest of his life, and in time it would shape the school that he built.

In 1878, feeling that his education was incomplete, Booker left Malden for Washington, where he spent several months studying at Wayland Seminary. It was his first long stay in a great city, and he looked at everything with the sharp attention of a young man who had been poor and was determined to learn. The capital was, in its own way, a school in itself, and the lessons it taught were not all found in the classroom.

In Washington he observed a number of young men who spent borrowed money on elegant clothes and carriage rides while they waited for jobs in the government offices, and he formed the opinion that they were living above their means. They seemed to him to have confused the appearance of success with the thing itself, and he thought they would have been far happier with a practical skill. He kept the lesson carefully in his mind, and he would use it many times in the years that followed.

For a time Booker considered whether he ought to become a minister, since the pulpit was a respected path for educated young Black men, and the thought was by no means a foolish one. He prayed, he talked with friends and he read widely, but no clear answer came to him. His real calling, though he did not know it yet, was waiting at the end of another road.

Towards the end of the school year, a letter arrived from General Armstrong, who invited his former pupil to return to Hampton in June 1879 to deliver the address to the graduating class. Booker was delighted and a little alarmed, for he knew that his old teachers and the visitors from the North would be listening critically. He resolved to prepare the speech more thoroughly than anything he had ever written.

On the day itself Booker stood before the great hall at Hampton, filled with students, teachers and distinguished guests, and delivered his speech with a clear voice and a steady hand. The audience listened closely, and he felt, for the first time, the strange and thrilling power of holding a room in silence. It was not yet the famous speech that would one day make him known across the country, but it was the first of many great occasions.

Soon afterwards General Armstrong told him that he wished him to return to Hampton as a member of the staff, with two tasks that would test his patience and his judgment. He was to take charge of a group of young Native American students, and he was also to organise a night school for poor students who could not afford to attend by day. Booker accepted at once, and the General, who had been waiting for his answer, was clearly very pleased.

A number of young Native Americans, from tribes of the western plains, had come to Hampton, and they lived in a building called the Wigwam, where Booker took up residence as their house father. He thought of the work as an experiment, and he was proud to be trusted with it. Within a few weeks he had become a familiar and respected figure among them, and he did his best to be worthy of that respect.

The Native students came from several different nations, and many of them could speak little English, so Booker taught them the language patiently, one word at a time. Hampton required them to wear its clothes and follow its rules, which was a great change, and historians today often criticise such schools for taking young people so far from their own languages and families. Booker observed that Native students were sometimes admitted to places where he, as a Black man, was turned away, and he found the injustice hard to explain.

At the same time Booker started a night school for the young men and women who had no money for fees and therefore worked all day in the school's shops and fields, studying only in the evening. They came to be called the Plucky Class, and the name was well earned, because they came to their lessons exhausted but unbeaten. Booker admired them enormously, and he never forgot the example of their quiet and stubborn courage.

The Plucky Class was a spectacular success, and General Armstrong, who noticed everything, became more and more confident in the young teacher he had trained. Booker, for his part, was entirely happy at Hampton, surrounded by friends he loved and work he believed in, and it never crossed his mind that he might one day leave. He supposed that he would spend his whole life there, but fate had other plans.

In the small Alabama town of Tuskegee, two men had long dreamed of a school for Black children. One was Lewis Adams, a skilled tinsmith who had been born into slavery and had become a leader of his community, and the other was George Campbell, a white businessman who respected education. Neither had much money, but both had patience and local influence, and together they set a remarkable chain of events in motion.

According to historians, Adams helped to win the votes of Black citizens for a candidate who promised to support a school. When that candidate won, the Alabama legislature voted two thousand dollars a year for teachers' salaries at a new normal school in Tuskegee. It was a small sum, and it did not include a single cent for land, buildings or books, but in 1881 it was all they had.

Adams and Campbell wrote to General Armstrong at Hampton, asking him to recommend a principal for the new school. They plainly expected him to name a white man, since in that time and place it seemed unthinkable that a Black man could be put in charge. Their letter, though they could not know it, would prove to be one of the most fortunate that they ever wrote.

Armstrong, who had known Booker for years and admired him deeply, answered that he could not recommend any white man for the post. He did, however, suggest a young Black teacher at Hampton who might be exactly the person they needed, and he described Booker's character, training and gift for teaching. It was a daring suggestion, and he made it without a moment's hesitation, as if the matter had been settled long before.

A few days afterwards a telegram arrived from Alabama, and the message was brief and decisive. Booker T Washington, it declared, would suit them perfectly, and he should be sent to Alabama at once without any delay. Booker was astonished, because he had never thought of leading a school of his own, and he read the telegram twice before he truly believed what it said.

Booker was only about twenty-five years old, and he had never been responsible for an institution, let alone one that did not yet exist. He was proud to have been chosen, but he was also uneasy about the weight of the task that lay ahead. He said goodbye to General Armstrong with deep gratitude, and the old General, he says, was confident enough for both of them.

In the early summer of 1881 Booker travelled south by train into Alabama, gazing out of the carriage window at the unfamiliar fields and forests for hours without speaking. Every mile took him farther from the world that he knew and nearer to a task that he could scarcely imagine. He was going, though he did not yet realise it, to the real beginning of his life's work.

Tuskegee lay in what was called the Black Belt, a region whose name came partly from the dark, fertile soil and partly from the large Black population that lived there. In that part of Alabama, Black families outnumbered white ones by a great margin, and most of them were poor farmers who rented their land. It was precisely the sort of place that stood in the greatest need of a school, and Booker was about to discover how great that need was.

When Booker arrived in Tuskegee, he went to look for the school and discovered, to his dismay, that nothing of the kind existed. There was no land, no building, no equipment and not a single pupil, and the state had promised money for teachers' salaries and nothing else. Many men in his position would have turned round and gone straight home, but Booker was not one of them.

The only premises that the townspeople could offer him were an old church called Butler Chapel, with a leaking roof, and a miserable shanty standing next to it, and neither was fit to hold a school. Booker examined them with a steady eye and decided that, poor as they were, they would serve for the time being. It was a small and inauspicious beginning, but he had never expected anything else.

Before opening the school, Booker spent a month travelling about the countryside by cart, visiting cabins and plantations and talking to anyone who would speak to him. He wanted to understand how the people actually lived before he decided what a school should teach them. It was a sensible beginning, and it proved the most valuable month of preparation he could have had.

He entered many one-room cabins in which an entire family slept, cooked and ate in a single room, and where the daily meal was frequently little more than salt pork and cornbread. The people received him with warmth, sharing what they had and asking eager questions about the new school. He noticed that hardly any of them owned a book, a table fit for a meal or a bed that was not a heap of rags.

In one cabin he found a handsome organ standing in the corner of a room that had almost nothing else. When he asked about it, he learned that the family had bought it on credit and that nobody in the house could play it, and the purchase seemed to him typical of a poverty that confused show with real value. He thought sadly of how the same money might have bought a stove, a bed or a few acres of land.

Booker also learned how many farmers lived under a system of credit, renting their land and buying food, seed and tools on account at the local store, at prices that rose steeply with the interest. When the cotton was sold at harvest time, the greater part of the money went to settle the debt, and the family began the next year in exactly the same position. He saw clearly that a problem of this kind would never be solved by reading and writing alone, however much they were valued.

The country schools that he visited were usually open for only a few months of the year, and they met in log cabins with dirt floors, few benches and almost no books. The teachers, who were poorly paid, had in many cases received hardly any education themselves, and the children walked miles to sit in these cold rooms. Booker saw at once why teachers with a better education, and with practical knowledge of country life, were so badly needed.

After many conversations over fences and around kitchen fires, Booker concluded that his school must teach people how to live, farm, build and save, as well as how to read and write. A school that taught only from books, he thought, would do little to change the lives of people so deeply bound to the land. That single idea, simple as it sounds, would shape nearly every decision that he made in the long years that followed.

On 4 July 1881, the Tuskegee Normal School opened its doors in the old church and the shabby little house that stood beside it, and for the moment Booker was the only teacher. He had very little furniture and hardly any books, yet he did have a roomful of students who were ready to learn, and that was what mattered most. Everything else, he told himself, could be built afterwards, one step at a time.

About thirty students arrived on the first day, and they were not children but grown men and women, ranging in age from fifteen to forty. Many of them were teachers already, who had come to improve their own knowledge so that they could return to their country schools and teach others better. It was an inspiring group of people, and Booker was deeply moved by the seriousness with which they approached their lessons.

Booker soon discovered that many of his students could recite facts from books but knew little about the ordinary habits of a clean and healthy life. He therefore insisted that each of them should bathe regularly, keep a tidy bed and own a toothbrush, which he called an important sign of civilisation. These lessons, he was convinced, were as valuable as any that came out of a textbook.

Soon after the school opened, a gifted young teacher named Olivia Davidson arrived to join him, and the school suddenly had two teachers where it had had only one. She had been trained at Hampton and at a normal school in Massachusetts, and she brought tireless energy and a remarkable talent for winning friends. Booker gave her much of the credit for the school's survival in its first difficult years.

The cramped church and shanty were soon too small for the growing school, and when an abandoned plantation of about a hundred acres came up for sale on the edge of town, Booker determined to buy it. He had almost no money, but he was convinced that the school would never prosper without land of its own on which to grow. The idea was bold, and perhaps a little reckless, but it was exactly the kind of daring that the school's early days demanded.

Booker wrote to General Marshall, the treasurer at Hampton, explaining the situation and asking for a loan to make the first payment on the property. Marshall, who had confidence in the young principal, sent five hundred dollars without delay, and the gift felt like the opening of a door. Booker never forgot the trust that the loan represented, and he resolved that every dollar of it would be repaid with honour.

The farm was in a sorry state, for years of cotton growing had exhausted the soil, deep gullies scarred the slopes and thick brush had swallowed the old fields. The big house had burned to the ground long before, and only a few humble buildings remained: a kitchen, a stable and a hen-house, all of them in need of repair. It was not a promising inheritance for a school, yet to Booker's eyes every worn-out acre was full of possibility.

Many of the students looked at the neglected hillside with dismay, since they had come to Tuskegee to study books and they did not see why they should be doing farm labour. Some had cherished the hope that education would lift them out of the fields for good, and the idea of returning to them was bitterly disappointing. Booker understood their feelings very well, but he had no intention of changing his plan, and he set about winning them over.

His answer was not an argument but an example, for he picked up an axe and a bush hook with his own hands and began to cut down the thorny undergrowth himself. The students looked on in surprise as their principal laboured in old clothes, and little by little they took up their own tools and joined him. By the end of the first day, the work had become a shared enterprise.

For weeks the students hacked at the brush, piled the branches into great heaps, burned them and dug out stubborn roots from the red earth. It was heavy work under a hot Alabama sun, and blisters and aching backs were common, but the overgrown hillside began slowly to look like farmland again. Every cleared acre was a small triumph for which they had paid in sweat.

When the ground was ready, the students ploughed it and planted crops of vegetables and corn, and they were taught how to do the work properly rather than simply being ordered to do it. The harvest helped to feed the school, and the lessons in the field were as real as any in the classroom. In this way the farm began to pay for itself, as well as to teach.

The old kitchen, the stable and the hen-house were scrubbed, whitewashed and furnished with rough benches, and they became classrooms and workshops for the growing school. These buildings were humble in the extreme, and the smell of the animals lingered in them for some time. Even so, they gave the students more space than they had ever had in the crowded church.

Olivia Davidson proved to be a gifted organiser, and she arranged suppers, festivals and entertainments in the town to raise money for the school. Black and white neighbours came to them, mixing in a way that was unusual in Alabama at that time, and every dollar that was collected went to pay for the land and the buildings. Her work did as much to build goodwill among the neighbours as it did to fill the school's empty treasury.

There were many nights when Booker lay awake going over the figures in his head, for the school owed money on the land, and the payments came around with a dreadful regularity. Yet each morning the sight of students working on the hillside and the generosity of the neighbours restored his courage, and he would rise ready to begin again. Fear and faith, he found, could share the same bed, and it was faith that usually had the last word.

The old kitchen and the hen-house were no longer adequate for the growing school, and Booker was determined to give it a proper building at a price that it could afford. His solution was daring: the students would make the bricks themselves, and in doing so they would acquire a trade and save the cost of buying them. It was the first great gamble of Tuskegee's early years, and it came very close to costing the young school its good name.

They dug red clay from the school's land, mixed it with water, pressed it into wooden moulds and set the soft bricks out in long rows to dry in the sun. Everything went well until the question of burning arose, for nobody among them, not even the principal, knew how a kiln should be built or fired. They would have to learn by their own mistakes, and the mistakes were soon to come.

They stacked the dried bricks into a great kiln and lit the fires beneath, hoping for the best, but the kiln failed, and when they opened it, most of the bricks were spoiled. Weeks of digging, shaping and waiting had been thrown away in a single disappointing hour. The students stood in silence for a long while, looking at the wreckage of everything that they had worked so hard to make.

Undaunted, Booker had a second kiln built, and the whole process began again, with new bricks and new hopes. This kiln failed too, and some doubters began to say that a school had no business trying to make bricks at all. Even the students, who had worked so hard and so cheerfully, were by now tired, hungry and thoroughly discouraged.

Booker had no money for another attempt, and so he took his watch to a pawnbroker, borrowed fifteen dollars on it and used the money to pay for a third kiln. It was a considerable sacrifice for a man who owned so little, but he believed that the school's future was worth more than any timepiece. He gave the watch up without complaint, and the work began once more with a new kiln, a fresh supply of clay and a little less hope than before.

This time the students tended the fires day and night, taking turns in the red glow of the kiln, and Booker shared the anxious watch. Nobody dared to sleep for long, because a single mistake in the heat might undo everything, and the strain was felt by all. It was the most anxious week that the little school had yet known, and nobody who was there forgot it.

When the kiln had at last cooled, the students opened it carefully and peered inside, hardly daring to look. The bricks were hard, red and sound, and a great shout of joy went up from everyone watching, since after two failures the success seemed almost miraculous. After so many weeks of failure and worry, a plain red brick had never looked so beautiful to anyone who stood there.

Before long Tuskegee was selling its bricks to the people of the town, and the brickyard soon became a useful source of income. It also gave the students a chance to learn a trade for which there was constant demand all over the South, where there were many buildings to be built. Many of the buildings that rose in Tuskegee over the following years were built from bricks made on the school's own land.

Students who learned to make bricks acquired a skill that they could use wherever they went, and they carried their pride with them into the world after leaving the school. Booker was more convinced than ever that learning by doing real and useful work taught more, and taught it more deeply, than any lecture. Tuskegee was beginning to teach the lesson that it would repeat for generations of students, in field, workshop and classroom alike.

With good bricks now at their disposal, Booker could finally plan the school's first large building, and the students began by digging a long, deep trench for the foundation. They worked with enthusiasm, knowing that they were laying the base of their own school with their own hands. It was no longer a dream on a hillside, but a building that was beginning to take shape.

A generous friend of the school in Brooklyn, a Mr Porter, sent a gift of money for the first large building that Tuskegee would ever have, and the hall was to carry his name. The gift arrived at a moment when Booker was beginning to despair of ever raising enough, and he received it with deep relief. It was a new kind of help, since it came from a stranger who simply believed in the idea.

The students laid the walls with the bricks they had made themselves, learning the mason's craft one course at a time, as the structure rose slowly above the foundation. Booker believed that there was no better lesson in bricklaying than building a real wall that would stand for generations. Every student who worked there carried away not only a skill but a pride in good work.

In the carpentry shop, other students sawed timber, planed boards and fitted doors and window frames, and they were learning a valuable trade while they made the actual parts of the building. They worked under the eye of skilled instructors, and Booker made sure that each piece was properly finished before it was used. Here, as everywhere at Tuskegee, learning and building went hand in hand, and each made the other worth doing.

Lumber, nails, glass and hardware all had to be paid for, and Booker was constantly walking the narrow line between the money he had and the money that he owed. He made it a rule to pay every bill as soon as he could, for he knew that an honest reputation was the school's most valuable possession. In time, the merchants of the district came to trust him, because he had never once failed to keep his word to them.

Week by week the walls of the new building climbed higher, and the whole school gathered to watch them rise against the Alabama sky. The students felt a special pride in the structure, since every brick, board and nail had come from their own labour or their own land. It was a living lesson in what patient, collective effort could achieve, and it was one that no textbook could have taught so well.

At last Porter Hall was completed, a solid brick building with classrooms, offices and rooms for living, and it stood on the hill like a promise kept. The students filed into it with a mixture of reverence and delight, because they knew that no one had built it for them, and that they had built it themselves. It was a moment of quiet triumph for the entire school, and none of those who were present ever forgot it.

When the building was ready, there were no beds in it, and so the students made their own, stuffing cloth sacks with straw to form mattresses and fixing rough wooden frames. They joked that they had to make their beds before they could lie in them, and the saying became a favourite one at the school. Booker thought the joke contained a great deal of truth about the way a person rises.

Booker believed that a school should teach ordinary habits of civilised life as well as formal lessons, so he insisted that meals be eaten at proper tables, with cloths, plates and good manners. For many of the students, who had grown up eating from a single dish or with their fingers, it was a new and rather comical experience. Yet within a few weeks the dining room had become a real classroom in its own right.

In 1882 Booker married Fannie Smith, a young woman from Malden whom he had known since his boyhood, and she came to live with him at the school and shared the labours of its early years. She was a patient and cheerful companion in a time that demanded patience, and Booker was grateful for her help. For a short while, in the midst of so much labour and anxiety, their small home was a very happy one indeed.

Their daughter, Portia, was born in 1883, and the new father's joy was complete, for it seemed that his private life was now as full of promise as his work. Fannie fell ill, however, and she died about two years after the wedding, leaving Booker with a baby daughter and a heavy sorrow. He returned to his duties because the school needed him, and because work was the only comfort that he could find.

Olivia Davidson travelled north again and again, speaking in churches and drawing rooms and appealing for help, and she returned each time with gifts that kept the school alive. Her health was frail, yet her energy seemed to know no limit, and she charmed even those who had little interest in education. Booker never ceased to wonder at the spirit that burned inside such a delicate frame.

After some years Booker and Olivia were married, and they had two sons together, and the family lived on the school grounds in the midst of their work. She went on teaching, planning and raising money while caring for her children, and she gave all her strength to the school and to her home alike. It was a heavy load for one person to carry, and it was carried with a smile.

In 1889 Olivia died, worn out by years of unceasing labour and illness, and the whole community fell into mourning for the woman who had done more than anyone to build the school beside Booker. He lost a wife, a colleague and a friend in a single stroke, and he was left with two young sons and an empty house. Yet the school had to be kept going, and he returned to his work.

That same year a new teacher arrived in Tuskegee, Margaret Murray, a graduate of Fisk University, who took the post of Lady Principal and became responsible for the education of the school's young women. She was strong, capable and deeply devoted to the work, and in time she would become much more than a colleague to Booker. The school gained an indispensable leader in the very year that it lost a great one.

Warren Logan, a Hampton graduate, joined the staff during the early years and became the school's treasurer, keeping its accounts with a care that was a comfort to everyone. Like all the other teachers, he worked for a small salary, and he did it out of loyalty to the cause rather than for any hope of reward. The school owed much of its steadiness in those uncertain years to such quiet and faithful people, whose names were seldom heard outside its walls.

Each evening the students gathered in the chapel for prayers, and they sang the old spirituals that their parents and grandparents had known in slavery, in voices of astonishing richness. The songs, sorrowful and triumphant at once, became a loved tradition of Tuskegee, and visitors who came from far away remembered the singing long after they had forgotten the speeches. For the students, it was a way of honouring where they had come from.

On his many journeys, Booker was sometimes refused a hotel room or a seat in a railway carriage because of his colour, and he faced these insults without any show of bitterness. He resolved that he would never allow any man to narrow his soul by making him hate, for hatred, he believed, poisons the person who feels it far more than the person who is hated. This calm refusal to be provoked became one of the chief sources of his influence.

Booker made a habit of walking about the campus and visiting the students' rooms himself. He believed that small details, such as a swept path, a made bed or a tidy shelf, revealed more about a school than any number of fine speeches. Some students dreaded his inspections, but in time nearly all of them came to understand why he cared so much about such things.

At Tuskegee every student had to work with his hands every day, whether in the fields, the shops or the kitchens, and the labour counted towards the cost of the student's education. This system allowed young people who had no money to attend at all, and it also taught them the dignity and the discipline of useful work. Booker regarded this arrangement as the very heart of the school, and he defended it against all those who wished that the students would spend their days on books alone.

Following the example of Hampton, Tuskegee also opened a night school for students who could not afford the full fees, and these students laboured for the school all day and went to class in the evening. They arrived tired but determined, with the dust of the fields or the workshop still on their clothes, and their classmates admired them greatly. In their quiet sacrifice, Booker saw the true spirit of the whole enterprise, and he held it up as an example to everyone who passed through the school.

The school's needs seemed endless, since land, buildings and teachers' salaries all had to be paid for, and the poor people of Macon County could give little. Booker therefore spent many months of each year travelling north by train, asking for help from those who were able to give it. It was a task that he found tiring and humbling, but he accepted it as part of his work.

In churches, lecture halls and the parlours of private houses, he told the story of the school in plain and simple words, avoiding any trace of begging or complaint. He found that people responded best when they were treated as intelligent partners in a worthwhile enterprise rather than as targets for appeals. His modest manner persuaded many listeners who would almost certainly have ignored a louder or more forceful speaker.

Booker kept honest accounts, and he was always able to show his supporters exactly how their money had been spent and what it had achieved. He invited donors to come to Tuskegee and see for themselves, for he believed that people give most generously when they can see results with their own eyes. This open and orderly method earned him a reputation for trustworthiness that was worth more than any sum.

Many doors stayed closed, and many people who listened politely sent him away with nothing, since there was always some reason why this was not the right time. Booker learned not to take refusals personally, and he often returned the following year to try again, until a first refusal turned into a modest gift. His patience, which had been tested so often by the work of the school, became one of the most useful tools that he possessed.

One of the gifts that moved him most came from a very different kind of donor, an elderly woman named Aunt Caroline Smith, who had been born into slavery and had almost nothing in the world. She had no money to offer, but she brought six eggs, which she presented to the school as her contribution, saying that she wished to help. It was a small gift, yet in its own way it was worth more than many far larger ones, because it was everything that she had to give.

Booker wrote a letter of thanks to every person who gave, whether the sum was a few cents or many hundreds of dollars, and he did it promptly and with obvious sincerity. He believed that kindness deserved to be answered warmly, and that gratitude was the beginning of a lasting friendship between a school and its supporters. Many of those early donors remained faithful to Tuskegee for the rest of their lives.

Gradually, travellers from the North began to come south to see the school for themselves, and they walked about the grounds and watched the students at their work in the fields, the shops and the classrooms. Many of them arrived as curious strangers and left as enthusiastic friends of Tuskegee, promising help when they returned home. It was the most persuasive form of advertisement that the school could have had.

A fund called the Slater Fund, established to help in the education of freed people, began in later years to make grants to Tuskegee, which helped the school to pay its teachers. Such institutions gave a degree of stability that private gifts alone could not provide. Booker was grateful for such friends, but he took care never to depend on any single source.

The constant travelling was exhausting, for Booker rode the night trains, waited in cold stations and slept in cramped seats, and he often arrived at his meetings weary to the bone. Yet every journey brought either money or friends, and each dollar meant another bed, another bench or another student who could stay at the school. That simple thought carried him through many a long and uncomfortable night on the road, and it never failed to cheer him.

As gifts arrived from the North, new buildings began to appear beside Porter Hall, among them dormitories and workshops, and each one was built largely by the students themselves. The campus changed year by year, from a few humble buildings on a bare hillside to a small and busy community. Booker looked at it all with a gratitude that he found hard to express in words.

As the years went by, Tuskegee added one trade after another, until students could learn carpentry, blacksmithing, printing, shoemaking, harness making, tailoring and many other crafts. Most of them worked at real jobs for the school, producing furniture, clothing and goods that were actually used. The workshops were as busy as any factory, and they were also classrooms in their own way.

In 1892 Robert Taylor, a trained Black architect who had studied at a leading technical institute in the North, joined the school as a teacher, and he drew the plans for many of its buildings. The students constructed them under his direction, so that each new hall became both a building and a lesson in building. Taylor's work gave the campus a dignity and a unity that the early huts and sheds had never had, and the students were proud of it.

Booker had long been troubled by the poverty and debt of the farmers around him, and he decided to invite them to Tuskegee for a meeting at which they could talk freely among themselves. His reasoning was that neighbours who shared their problems might discover answers that no outside expert could give them. It was a simple idea, but it was one that no one had tried before.

In February 1892 about four hundred men and women, many of them poor farmers, some of whom had never set foot in a school, travelled to Tuskegee for the first Negro Conference by wagon, mule and on foot. They filled the hall, with the dust of the roads still on their clothes, and waited with a mixture of curiosity and suspicion. Booker knew that the success of the day would depend on whether they felt welcome.

Booker asked them plain and practical questions about whether they owned their land or rented it, whether they owed money to the store, and whether their children went to school for more than a few weeks of the year. The farmers answered truthfully, and many were struck by what their own answers revealed. For the first time, the whole problem was laid out in front of them in plain view.

One by one the farmers stood up to speak about debt, rents and the crops that paid best, and they talked with a frankness that astonished the teachers who listened. They had never before been asked for their opinions in such a setting, and they seized the opportunity with enthusiasm. Some of their stories were funny, and some were heartbreaking, but all of them were true.

The farmers went home with practical ideas about saving money, buying land, building better houses and avoiding debt, and many of them resolved to change their ways. The conference became an annual event and grew larger each year, and the example was followed in other parts of the South. It was a modest gathering, held in a simple hall, yet in time its example reached far beyond the walls of the school.

General Armstrong had been in poor health for some time, and in the spring of 1893 he died, at the age of only fifty-four. Booker was overcome with sorrow, because he had lost the man who had been his teacher, his model and his dearest friend, and he felt the loss more deeply than he could easily say. He had never really imagined that he would one day have to carry on his work without him.

As he had wished, the General was buried in the Hampton cemetery among the students whom he had loved and served, and Booker attended the funeral with a heavy heart. He thought of all that he had learned from that great man, of unselfish service, of faith in work and of courage in the face of difficulty. He promised himself that he would continue the General's work as faithfully as he could.

In 1893 Booker married Margaret Murray, who had been Lady Principal at Tuskegee since 1889 and who had proved herself a gifted and devoted teacher. She became his steady partner for the rest of his life, caring for his children and leading the school's work for women with skill and imagination. Booker's home, which had known so much sorrow, was once again filled with warmth.

In 1895 the city of Atlanta planned a great fair, the Cotton States and International Exposition, to show the world how far the South had recovered from the war. The organisers hoped to attract Northern money and Northern visitors to the city, and they set aside a special building to display the work of Black Americans. They also knew that they would need the support of Black citizens if the fair was to be a real success.

Some time earlier, Booker had spoken in Washington before a committee of Congress in support of the Exposition, and the men from Atlanta who heard him were impressed by the calm and honest way in which he spoke. He did not know it at the time, but that appearance before the committee would change the whole course of his life. It had planted in the minds of the organisers the idea of asking him to speak at the opening of the fair itself, in front of the whole country.

The directors of the Exposition invited Booker to speak at the opening ceremony, and the invitation was an honour of a kind that few Black Americans had ever received in the South. He accepted with gratitude, although he understood perfectly well how heavy the responsibility would be. He was being asked to speak for millions of people, and to do it in front of those who had been their masters.

Booker knew that he would be speaking to two audiences at once, one Black and one white, and that each of them had its own fears about what he might say. Many Black listeners feared that he would say too little, and many white listeners feared that he would say too much. Whichever way he turned, he was in danger of disappointing someone, and he knew that a single careless sentence might be remembered for years.

He wrote the speech with the greatest possible care, crossing out sentences and weighing every word until at last it expressed what he wanted to say. His aim was to tell the truth as he saw it while winning the goodwill of everyone in the room. It was a task that required both courage and tact in almost equal measure, and he knew it.
