The teachers and students at Tuskegee wished him luck and stood waving as his train pulled out of the station. Booker slept very little on the journey, because his mind kept returning to the speech and to the thousands of people who would be waiting. He arrived in Atlanta with a calm face and a restless heart, and he was thankful that nobody could see which of the two was telling the truth.

On the opening day the streets of Atlanta were bright with banners and loud with bands, and the sun beat down on the crowds that were making their way to the Exposition grounds. Everywhere there was the feeling of a great occasion, and the whole South seemed to have turned out to take part. Booker walked through it all with his speech folded in his pocket, feeling both exhilarated and slightly sick with nerves.

Booker took his place on a high platform among governors, officials and Southern leaders, and he was one of the first Black men ever invited to speak at such an event. He later confessed that his heart was beating so loudly that he could hardly hear himself think. Below him, the vast hall was filled with thousands of expectant faces, both Black and white.

Governor Rufus Bullock rose to introduce the speaker, and he called Booker a representative of Negro civilisation, a phrase that drew applause from the great crowd in the hall. The moment was solemn, and a little strange, because many in the audience had never before heard a Black man speak from such a platform. Booker rose from his chair and walked slowly to the front of the platform, aware that this was the moment for which he had been preparing for weeks.

A hush fell over the hall as Booker stood up, and he waited for a moment before speaking, looking out over the sea of faces. In a clear and steady voice, he began by reminding the audience that one third of the people of the South were Black, and that no enterprise could succeed if it ignored them. It was a simple fact, but it fell upon the room like a bell.

Booker began by telling the crowd that one third of the people of the South were Black, and that no plan for the region's future could succeed if it ignored them. He argued that both races were bound together in the same land, and that they would rise or fall together. It was a message of shared interest rather than complaint, and it was cleverly chosen for his mixed audience.

Then he told a story about a ship that had been lost at sea for many days, whose crew, dying of thirst, saw another vessel and signalled desperately for water. The answer came back across the waves: “Cast down your bucket where you are.” Again and again the thirsty sailors signalled, and again and again they received the very same reply, which must have seemed to them a strange and unkind joke.

At last the captain of the stricken ship did as he was told and lowered his bucket, and it came up full of fresh, sparkling water. The vessel, as it happened, was floating at the mouth of the great Amazon River, and the sea around it was sweet. The audience, who had been listening closely, understood that this was no ordinary story, and that its meaning was about to be applied to the South.

Turning to the Black members of his audience, Booker urged them to cast down their buckets where they were, in farming, in the trades, in housework, in business and in the professions. He asked them to make friends with the people around them and to make themselves useful to their communities, building their strength patiently, brick by brick. Many in the hall were moved by his words, and some were uneasy about what he had left unsaid.

Then he addressed the white members of the audience, begging them to look to the Black neighbours who had worked their fields, cleared their forests and built their railroads. These were people whom they already knew and had tested over many years, he said, and he urged them to rely on them rather than on strangers from distant countries. It was a shrewd appeal to self-interest as well as to justice, and it was made with great courtesy.

Holding up his hand, with the fingers spread, he declared that in all things purely social the two races could be as separate as the fingers, yet as one hand in everything essential to the progress of all. The image was memorable and persuasive, and it brought a long wave of applause. He also dismissed agitation for social equality as foolish, and this was the sentence that his critics would never forgive.

He went on to say that no people could prosper until they learned that there was as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem. It was at the bottom of life, he insisted, and not at the top, that a people had to begin its climb. The sentence summed up the philosophy of his whole career, and it struck a chord with farmers, workers and teachers alike across the country.

When he finished, the hall exploded into cheers, and people rose to their feet, waving hats and handkerchiefs in a storm of excitement. Governor Bullock rushed across the platform and seized Booker's hand, and the applause rolled on for what seemed an age. The speech had been a triumph far beyond anything that Booker himself had dared to hope for, and he knew it.

Within a day or two, newspapers across the country were printing long extracts from the address, and Northern editors wrote about it with warm approval, as did many in the South. President Grover Cleveland wrote to congratulate him on the speech and to thank him for sending a copy. Overnight, the principal of a small Alabama school had become one of the best-known Black men in America.

Not everyone cheered, however, and a number of Black leaders felt that Booker had given up too much, because he seemed to accept for the present the loss of voting rights and equal treatment. W E B Du Bois, who first wrote to congratulate him, later became one of his sharpest critics and called the speech a compromise. Booker believed that patient work was the wisest road, and the argument between the two views has never really ended.

In 1896 Harvard University awarded Booker an honorary degree, an honour that was rare for a Black American in those years, and it was said to be the first of its kind that the university had given to a Black man. The former salt packer walked across the famous yard in an academic gown, and he was conscious that it was a recognition of his school, not just of himself. He wore it with quiet pride, and he thought often of the janitor's broom that had once been his entrance ticket.

That same autumn George Washington Carver, a trained scientist who had been born into slavery and had earned a master's degree in Iowa, accepted Booker's invitation to come to Tuskegee and teach agriculture. Booker had warned him honestly that he could offer little money and no fame, only hard work and the chance to help many people. Carver accepted the offer gladly, and he would stay at Tuskegee for nearly half a century, until the end of his life.

Carver made a laboratory out of simple things, using jars and scraps that he had found. He taught the farmers of Alabama how to rest their exhausted soil by planting crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes in place of cotton. He also wrote bulletins in plain language, so that even poor farmers could use his advice, and his work gave Tuskegee a new and practical reputation.

By now Booker had thought a good deal about the art of speaking in public, and he shared his conclusions with the students. A speaker, he said, must have something real to say, must forget himself in his subject, and must talk plainly and warmly to his audience, as to a single friend rather than a crowd. It was advice that he had learned from experience, and it was given with a smile.

In October 1898, Booker was invited to speak at a great peace celebration in Chicago, with President McKinley seated nearby, and he used the occasion to praise the Black soldiers who had fought in the war with Spain. The hall was packed to the doors, and the audience responded to his words with warm and generous applause. Everyone present could see that the principal of a small Alabama school had become a figure of real national importance.

In December 1898, President William McKinley visited Tuskegee, accompanied by several members of his cabinet, and the entire school turned out to greet them. Students lined the road in orderly files, the band played, and the whole town gathered to watch, as if a great holiday had been declared. The visit was a proof that Tuskegee had been noticed at the highest level.

The visitors watched the students at work in classrooms, shops and fields, and they inspected the buildings that the students themselves had erected. The President said generous words about the school, and Booker felt that the long labour of the previous years was at last being understood. It had been a long journey from the leaking church and the old hen-house.

By 1899 Booker was exhausted by years of ceaseless travelling, speaking and fundraising on behalf of the school. His friends, who could see that his health was suffering, urged him to take a long rest and helped to pay for a trip to Europe. In the spring he sailed with his wife, feeling guilty about leaving the school and yet excited at the thought of seeing so much that was new.

In Europe, Booker found that he was treated with courtesy in hotels, shops and on the street, and after the insults he had endured at home, the experience was a welcome and surprising relief. He travelled through several countries, met many interesting people and observed with sympathy how ordinary workers lived. The journey widened his mind as well as resting his body, and he came to think about his own country in a new way.

He returned to Tuskegee rested and thankful, and the students gave him a joyful welcome as he stepped from the train, cheering and waving their hats. His head was full of new ideas for the school, drawn from what he had seen abroad, and he threw himself into his duties again. The man who had gone away exhausted had come back with new energy, and the school soon felt the difference in everything that he did.

In 1900 Booker founded the National Negro Business League in Boston, a society for Black business owners who wished to meet, to share advice and to prove that they could prosper in trade. It was a natural development of his lifelong belief in self-help and in the power of property to give a people security. The League would grow, over the following years, into one of the most influential Black organisations of its day, with members in hundreds of towns.

Local branches of the League sprang up in many towns, and shop owners, farmers, bankers and craftsmen came together to exchange ideas and encouragement. Booker held that every successful Black business was a small victory for the whole community, because success of this kind was hard for anyone to ignore. The League gave the practical side of his philosophy a lasting organisation, and it outlived its founder by many years.

In 1900 Booker began to tell his life story in a series of chapters for a magazine, writing in snatched moments between travelling, speaking and the daily work of the school. Friends and editors helped him polish the manuscript, but the voice was unmistakably his own: modest, honest and shot through with a gentle humour. It was the voice of a man who would always rather understate his achievements than boast of them to the reader.

In 1901 the chapters were gathered into a book under the title Up From Slavery, and it was an immediate success, praised by reviewers on both sides of the Atlantic and eventually translated into many languages. Readers around the world followed the journey of the boy who had slept on rags and carried a spelling book, and found in it a story of hope. The book made Booker famous far beyond the borders of America, and it brought the story of his school to readers who had never heard of Alabama.

In October 1901, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Booker to dine at the White House, an occasion said to be the first on which a Black guest had sat at a meal there by presidential invitation. Many white Southern newspapers reacted with fury, but Black Americans and many Northern whites saw the invitation as a sign of respect. It showed how far Booker had come since the day he first swept a classroom.

Roosevelt sometimes consulted Booker about public appointments and about the affairs of Black Americans, and Booker's influence grew steadily as a result. His critics grew in number as well, and some of them claimed that he held too much power and was too patient in the face of injustice. Whether he used that influence wisely, and whether his patient approach was the best one available to him, is a question that historians still discuss.

In 1903, the scholar W E B Du Bois published a book that criticised Booker's approach as too slow and too willing to accept inequality in return for modest progress. In 1909 a group of reformers founded a new organisation that wished to fight directly and urgently for full civil rights, a goal that Booker's methods did not stress. These were serious arguments about the best road to equality, and historians have long observed that both sides contained a good deal of truth.

By 1915 Booker was worn out by decades of travelling, speaking and fundraising, and he collapsed while visiting New York, where doctors found that his illness was grave. He asked to be taken home to the South, and the train carried him to Tuskegee, where he died on 14 November at about the age of fifty-nine. He had spent the last of his strength on the school that he loved, and it was there, among his own people, that he wished to end his days.

Thousands of students, teachers, graduates and townspeople attended the funeral, and he was buried on the campus, not far from the red brick buildings that his students had made with their own hands. When he died, more than a thousand students were enrolled in the school that had started with thirty in a leaking church. The little school that had begun in a borrowed building had become one of the best-known institutions in America, and its founder's name was known around the world.

Today Tuskegee is a university, and part of its historic campus is a national historic site where visitors can walk among the buildings that the first students made, including the house that they built for Booker and his family. Up From Slavery is still widely read, admired for its courage and humour and challenged for its cautious politics, and its author remains one of the most debated figures in American history. Whatever one decides, it is hard not to be moved by the journey of a boy who carried books to a schoolhouse door and eventually opened one of his own.
